Results: All patients tolerated the intralymphatic immunotherapy (ILIT) treatment well, and the injections did not elicit any severe adverse event. Patients receiving active treatment displayed an initial increase in allergen-specific IgE level and peripheral T-cell activation. A clinical improvement in nasal allergic symptoms upon challenge was recorded along with a decreased inflammatory response in the nose. In addition, these patients reported an improvement in their seasonal allergic disease. No such changes were seen in the placebo group. Conclusions: Although this study is based on a limited number of patients, ILIT with grass-pollen or birch-pollen extracts appears to reduce nasal allergic symptoms without causing any safety problems. Hence, ILIT might constitute a less time-consuming and more cost-effective alternative to conventional subcutaneous allergen-specific immunotherapy. © 2013 American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology.
The relevance of patient-reported outcomes in a grass pollen immunotherapy trial in children and adolescents with rhinoconjunctivitis; Background: Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) are the only instruments available to assess the efficacy of an intervention in patients with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Methods: A previously published immunotherapy trial in children and adolescents (6-18yr) with hay fever provided us with data to assess the relevance of two of these additional outcome measures, the disease-specific rhinoconjunctivitis quality of life questionnaire (RQLQ) and the generic COOP/WONCA-charts (CWC). A PRO was considered relevant if it was responsive to pollen exposure and at least had a moderate correlation with the classical symptoms of allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Furthermore, we evaluated a post-season PRO, that is, a global assessment of symptoms (GAS). This assessment is used in clinical trials as a tool for selecting participants with sufficient symptoms and in daily practice to evaluate the patient's complaints during the preceding season. We assessed the correlation of this retrospective score with the actual symptoms during the previous pollen season. Results: Data from 36 children and 63 adolescents were analysed. On the basis of the total scores of the paediatric and adolescent version of the RQLQ, both questionnaires were considered relevant as they were responsive to exposure and showed a moderate to strong correlation with the rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms. However, in both children and adolescents, 40% of the RQLQ items were not relevant according to our definition. The CWC as a whole and the separate charts appear less relevant because of the weak correlations with the daily symptom score from the diary. The CWC are not relevant in the monitoring of children and adolescents with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis caused by grass pollen. Efficacy and safety of the SQ-standardized grass allergy immunotherapy tablet in mono- and polysensitized subjects; The efficacy of single-allergen-specific immunotherapy in polysensitized subjects is a matter of debate. We therefore performed a post hoc analysis of pooled data from six randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (N = 1871) comparing the efficacy and safety of the SQ-standardized grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT), Grazax (Phleum pratense 75 000 SQ-T/2800 BAU, ALK, Denmark), in mono- and polysensitized subjects. This was not dependent on sensitization status (P = 0.5772), suggesting a similar treatment effect in mono- and polysensitized subjects (i.e. reductions of the TCSs of 28% and 26%, respectively, both P < 0.0001). Finally, a comparable and favourable safety profile of grass AIT was demonstrated in the two subgroups. Thus, no difference in efficacy and safety of single-allergen grass AIT was observed between mono- and polysensitized subjects. © 2012 John Wiley & Sons A/S.

CONCLUSIONS: Propensity to treat broad-spectrum grass allergy is limited with an exemplar-based grass product.

Local nasal 'protective' immunoglobulin G4 (IgG4) responses in nasal fluid following grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy; RATIONALE: Grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) is associated with induction of serum IgG4-associated blocking antibodies that prevent IgE-facilitated allergen binding to B cells (IgE-FAB). We hypothesised that local nasal inhibitory IgG4 antibodies are also induced following SLIT. METHODS: Nasal fluids were obtained from SLIT-treated patients (n57), untreated allergics (n57) and non-atopic controls (n58). Specific IgE and IgG4 to Phleum pratense (Phl p) components were measured by ISAC microarray technology. Inhibitory activity of nasal fluid and serum was measured using the IgE-FAB assay. RESULTS: Untreated allergics had elevated levels of rPhl p 1 (p=0.01) and rPhl p 5-specific IgE in nasal fluid compared to non-atopic controls. SLIT-treated patients showed a trend for an increase in rPhl p 1 (mean+/-SE, 6.062.7 ISU) and rPhl p 5-specific IgE (2.162.6 ISU) compared to untreated allergics (p=0.12). Recombinant Phl p 5-specific IgG4 levels were increased in SLIT-treated patients compared to untreated allergics (p=0.02) and non-atopic controls (p=0.003). Inhibitory activity in nasal fluid for co-operative bindingof allergen-IgE complexes to B cells in SLIT-treated patients was significantly reduced (p=0.004) compared to untreated allergics. Interestingly, the magnitude of this suppression was more profound with local antibodies (45%) compared to the peripheral antibody responses (35%). Oralair®: A causal treatment for grass pollen-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis; Grass pollen-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis is a common disease, comprising more than just the classic symptoms of nasal obstruction, sneezing, rhinorrhea and itchy, watery eyes. Sufferers deal with severe impairments in daily life. Allergic rhinoconjunctivitis is also considered an important risk factor in the development of asthma. Allergen avoidance, medication for symptomatic treatment and allergen-specific immunotherapy are cornerstones in therapeutic management, but immunotherapy is the only available treatment that is able to affect the natural course of allergy. In recent decades, clinical trials have investigated the efficacy and safety of subcutaneous immunotherapy. To date, efforts have been made to develop more convenient routes of administration. Substantial improvement may be achieved through the application of sublingual tablets. This article discusses the development process of immunotherapy and the clinical background of the Oralair® (Stallergènes, Hauts-de-Seine, France) five-grass pollen tablet. Furthermore, it outlines this tablets efficacy and safety properties. © 2013 Future Medicine Ltd.
Medication persistence in children and young people on long-term, grass pollenspecific immunotherapy - Measured by prescription renewal rates; Background: Specific immunotherapy (SIT) is only successful if the patient continues treatment for the target duration of at least three years. To date, no studies on medication persistence in children and young people have been carried out under real-life conditions in Germany, e.g. based on prescription renewal rates. Objective: To determine, in a non-interventional study using prescription renewal rates for grass pollenspecific immunotherapy products, whether there is a difference in medication persistence between subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) and sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) in children and young people. Methods: Anonymised prescription renewals from children and young people on allergen immunotherapy consisting of SCIT with native allergens, SCIT with allergoids, and SLIT with native allergens were tracked for three consecutive years (2005 to 2007). Patients were classed as persistent if they had had at least one SIT prescription renewed per season in each of the three years. This study was a subgroup analysis of a cohort consisting of adults, adolescents and children. The results of the entire cohort have already been published. Results: The data from 562 children and young people aged 4 to 18 years were analysed. The overall persistence rate for SIT was 63.2% in year 2 and 44.1% in year 3. Analysing the modes of administration separately, the persistence rate in the second year was 74.1% for SLIT, 62.9% for SCIT with native allergens, and 61.1% for SCIT with allergoids. The figures for the third year were 57.4%, 40.6%, and 44.8%, respectively. In the third year, the difference between the SLIT group and the SCIT group with native allergens was significant (p = 0.024). Conclusions: Long-term use in children and young people is better with SLIT than SCIT with native or modified allergens. Overall, persistence with specific immunotherapy is better in the under-12s than in the 12 to 18 age group. The study does not allow any conclusions to be drawn on treatment adherence/compliance. © 2007 Dustri-Verlag Dr. Karl Feistle.
A systematic review and economic evaluation of subcutaneous and sublingual allergen immunotherapy in adults and children with seasonal allergic rhinitis; Background: Severe allergic rhinitis uncontrolled by conventional medication can substantially affect quality of life. Immunotherapy involves administering increasing doses of a specific allergen, with the aim of reducing sensitivity and symptomatic reactions. Recent meta-analyses have concluded that both subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) and sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) are more effective than placebo in reducing symptoms. It is uncertain which route of administration is more effective and whether or not treatment is cost-effective.Objective: To determine the comparative clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of SCIT and SLIT for seasonal allergic rhinitis in adults and children.Data sources: Electronic databases {MEDLINE, EMBASE, The Cochrane Library [Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL)], NHS Economic Evaluation Database (NHS EED)} and trial registries (from inception up to April 2011).Review methods: Standard systematic review methods were used for study selection, data extraction and quality assessment. Double-blind randomised, placebo-controlled trials of SCIT or SLIT, or of SCIT compared with SLIT, and economic evaluations were included. Meta-analysis and indirect comparison meta-analysis and meta-regression were carried out. A new economic model was constructed to estimate cost-utility.Results: Meta-analyses found statistically significant effects for SCIT and SLIT compared with placebo across a number of outcome measures and for the vast majority of subgroup analyses (type and amount of allergen, duration of treatment). There was less evidence for children, but some results in favour of SLIT were statistically significant. Indirect comparisons did not provide conclusive results in favour of either SCIT or SLIT. Economic modelling suggested that, when compared with symptomatic treatment (ST), both SCIT and SLIT may become cost-effective at a threshold of £20,000-30,000 per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) from around 6 years, or 5 years for SCIT compared with SLIT (NHS and patient perspective). Limitations: It is uncertain to what extent changes in the outcome measures used in the trials translate into clinically meaningful benefits. Cost-effectiveness estimates are based on a simple model, limited data and a number of assumptions, and should be seen as indicative only.Conclusions: A benefit from both SCIT and SLIT compared with placebo has been consistently demonstrated, but the extent of this effectiveness in terms of clinical benefit is unclear. Both SCIT and SLIT may be cost-effective compared with ST from around 6 years (threshold of £20,000-30,000 per QALY). Further research is needed to establish the comparative effectiveness of SCIT compared with SLIT and to provide more robust cost-effectiveness estimates. © Queen's Printer and Controller of HMSO 2013.

Heterogeneity of antibody responses among clinical responders during grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy.; During allergen-specific sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT), the relevance of changes in specific IgE and IgG antibody titres to treatment efficacy remains to be evaluated at an individual patient level. To investigate whether antibody responses can be used as biomarkers for SLIT efficacy. Comprehensive quantitative, qualitative and functional analyses of allergen-specific IgA, IgE, IgG1-4 and IgM responses were performed using purified Phl p 1 to 12 allergens in sera, saliva and nasal secretions from 82 grass pollen allergic patients. These patients were enrolled in a randomized, double-blind placebo-controlled study and assessed in an allergen challenge chamber (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00619827). Antibody responses were monitored in parallel to clinical responses before and after daily sublingual treatment for 4 months with either a grass pollen or a placebo tablet. A significant mean improvement (i.e. 33-40.6%) in rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom scores was observed in SLIT recipients, irrespective of their baseline patterns of IgE sensitization (i.e. narrow, intermediate, broad) to grass pollen allergens. SLIT did not induce any de novo IgE sensitization. Clinical responders encompassed both immunoreactive patients who exhibited strong increases in titres, affinity and/or blocking activity of grass-pollen-specific IgGs (representing 17% of treated patients), as well as patients with no detectable antibody responses distinguishing them from the placebo group. No significant changes were detected in antibody titres in saliva and nasal washes, even in clinical responders. Sublingual immunotherapy with a grass pollen tablet is efficacious irrespective of the patients' baseline sensitization to either single or multiple grass pollen allergens. Seric IgG responses may contribute to SLIT-induced clinical tolerance in a fraction (i.e. 17%) of patients, but additional immune mechanisms are involved in most patients. Consequently, antibody responses cannot be used as a marker of SLIT efficacy at an individual patient level. © 2013 John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Cellular effects of intralymphatic allergen-specific immunotherapy; Background: Allergen-specific immunotherapy is used to treat patients with IgE-mediated allergic disorders. Therefore, there is a need to reduce the duration and increase the attractiveness of the therapy. Recent evidence suggests that direct intralymphatic injections could yield a faster beneficial result with a lower allergen dose. In this double-blind placebo-controlled study we have evaluated the cellular effects of intralymphatic allergen-specific immunotherapy (ILIT). Method: Patients with pollen-induced allergic rhinitis were recruited and treated with three intralymphatic injections (with an interval of 4 weeks) of ALK Alutard (containing 1000 SQ-U birch- or grass-pollen) or placebo (ALK diluent). Result: All patients given ILIT tolerated the treatment well and did not suffer from any adverse events. Preliminary data suggest that patients having undergone ILIT display clinical improvement of nasal symptoms, lower levels of pulmonary NO and a decreased inflammatory response in the nose characterized by reduced numbers of cells and lowered levels of inflammatory mediators in nasal lavage fluids. Additionally, data on cells cultured with allergen in vitro points towards an enhanced proliferation of allergen-specific lymphocytes along with suppressed levels of activated granulocytes after completed treatment. Conclusion: ILIT appears to be safe for the patients and this treatment strategy seems to affect clinical parameters as well as the activation of granulocytes and mononuclear cells. Does sublingual immunotherapy work through the replacement of IgE epitopes?; Background: Grass pollen is a major cause of respiratory allergy worldwide. The aim of our study was to investigate the activity of specific IgE (sIgE) for Phleum epitopes in patients treated with grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT). Methods: Forty-one allergic patients to grass pollen were included in the study 26 patients received a pre-coseasonal grass SLIT for 2 years and 15 patients were used as controls. Eligible patients experienced symptoms of seasonal rhinoconjunctivitis during the previous year, positivity to Phleum skin prick tests and sIgE (>3.5 kU/l). Serum sIgE for Phleum and rPhl p1, rPhl p2, rPhl p5, rPhl p6, rPhl p7 and rPhl p12 were determined. Statistical analysis was performed by Wilcoxon and Fischer test. RAST-inhibition values for rPhl p1/rPhl p1, rPhl p1/rPhl p2, rPhl p1/ rPhl p4 and rPhl p2/rPhl p2, rPhl p2/rPhl p5 were measured. Results: Most patients showed high levels of rPhl p1 and rPhl p5 (mean>30 kU/l), and an intermediate level of rPhl p4 and rPhl p6 (mean>10 kU/l), while low or negative results were obtained for rPhl p2, rPhl p7 and rPhl p12 (mean<10 kU/l). Conversely to the control group, patients receiving SLIT increased their serum IgE for all epitopes except for rPhl p7 and rPhl p12. In patients undergoing SLIT, two groups were observed: the first group was characterized by a reduction of symptoms, the second showed similar symptoms or an increase. The analysis of rPhl p2/rPhl p5 ratio showed a significant increase only in patients who experienced a reduction in symptoms. No cross-reactivity between rPhl p1/rPhl p2 rPhl p1/rPhl p4 and rPhl p2/rPhl p5 was detected. Conclusion: Following 1 and 2 years of SLIT, in patients showing a clinical response a significant increase of sIgE for rPhl p2 and a less evident increase of sIgE for rPhl p1 and rPhl p5 were observed, highlighted also by the high increase in rPhl p2/rPhl p5 IgE ratio. These results suggest that SLIT is able not only to induce a TH2-TH1 isotopic switch, but also a mechanism of IgE epitope replacement.

Sublingual immunotherapy: Skin prick test changes in relation to clinical efficacy?; Background: Sublingual Immunotherapy is regarded as an effective treatment of allergic respiratory diseases. The aim of our study is to evaluate its clinical efficacy and to assess whether skin prick test sensitizations are modified after one year of treatment. Method: We selected 89 children aged between 6 and 15 years affected by rhinitis and/or asthma: 37 underwent SLIT for house dust mites (HDM) and 52 for grass mix (GM). For each patient nasal and bronchial symptoms were considered before treatment (T0) and after one year (T1). A score of 1 was assigned to mild symptoms, 2 to moderate and 3 to severe. Skin Prick tests (SPT) were performed at T0 and T1. Result: Children undergoing SLIT for HDM showed a decrease in both symptoms scores for rhinitis and asthma [from 5.7 ± 13.18 at T0 to 2.25 ± 2.47 at T1 (P < 0.001) for rhinitis and from 4.11 ± 1.98 to 1.65 ± 2.09 (P < 0.001) for asthma]. Patients with severe nasal symptoms were 22.6% at T0 and 3.2% at T1 while those with severe bronchial symptoms were 27% before the treatment and 8% after one year. No significant changes in SPT were reported for Dermatophagoides Farinae (Dpf) and Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus (Dpt). At T0 the mean wheal diameters were 7.47 ± 2.91 mm for Dpf and 7.13 ± 4.25 mm for Dpt whilst at T1 they became 6.56 ± 3.98 mm and 8.26 ± 4.25 mm respectively (P > 0.1). Moreover the reduction of symptom scores were verified also in children undergoing SLIT for GM [from 5.04 ± 2.03 at T0 to 2.25 ± 2.31 at T1 (P < 0.001) for rhinitis and from 4.66 ± 2.71 to 2.03 ± 2.37 (P < 0.001) for asthma]. Percentages of the subjects with high scores respectively decreased for their nasal and bronchial symptoms from 8.5% to 4.3% and from 36% to 15%. On the other hand also in this group the variation of skin reactivity was not statistically significant and the wheal size for Grass mix was 7.29 ± 3.71 mm at T0 and 7.59 ± 4.17 mm at T1 (P > 0.1). Conclusion: Sublingual Immunotherapy is effective in determining a reduction of asthma and rhinitis scores. Nevertheless this improvement of nasal and bronchial symptoms is not associated with the reduction of wheal size. SPT may not be a valid parameter to evaluate the clinical efficacy of SLIT after one year of treatment. Thus studies on larger cohorts of children are needed to assess if and when the suppression of skin reactivity takes place.
Economic evaluation of five-grass pollen tablets for the treatment of allergic rhinitis; Background: Allergen immunotherapy (AIT) is a pivotal treatment that is able to modify the natural history of allergy. The long experience developed in AIT allowed the development of five-grass pollen tablets, that are indicated for the treatment of grass-induced rhinoconjunctivitis (RC). A symptom score adjusted for rescue medication use, named 'AAdSS', has been recently introduced as a primary efficacy endpoint in grass pollen AIT RC trials. The real worth of the AAdSS relates to its ability to better estimate the true severity of symptoms by removing a source of bias (the use of rescue medication). Regarding five-grass pollen tablets the AAdSS was calculated a posteriori for two registrative clinical trials, the adult and pediatric. The differences in the AAdSS adjusted means for 300 IR vs placebo were -1.84 and -1.64, respectively. The aim of our study was to perform a cost-effectiveness analysis of five-grass pollen tablets from the Italian third party payer perspective, assembling the results of adult and long term trials together with economic data. Methods: According to national tariffs and standard drug prices in Italy, medical visits, diagnostic examinations, skin prick test, use of decongestants, intranasal drugs and oral antihistamines were valorized in euros. The Receiver Operating Curve (ROC) enabled us to assess the effectiveness of five-grass pollen tablets in terms of Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALY). A decision tree was also structured in order to model the possible outcomes and costs to a low, moderate and high AAdSS for adult and pediatric patients. A probabilistic sensitivity analysis was finally carried out to test the robustness of results as well as the consistency with an assumed costeffectiveness threshold of euros 30 000/ QALY. Results: The administration of five-grass pollen tablets costs 1024 euro/QALY with high and moderate AAdSS. Considering also the losses of productivity, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of adults becomes 700 euro/QALY. The 95% of the simulation performed in the probabilistic sensitivity analysis shows an ICER below the threshold of 30 000 euro/QALY. Conclusion: Our results demonstrate that five-grass pollen tablets represent a costeffective strategy in adults patients with moderate and severe AAdSS.

Persistence and compliance to grass immunotherapy treatment is comparable for SQ-standardised allergy immunotherapy tablets and subcutaneous immunotherapy: A Swedish registry study; Background: Allergy immunotherapy tablets (AITs) have been developed as an effective, well tolerated and convenient treatment modality, suitable for home administration. The purpose of this retrospective registry based study was to compare the persistence in use and compliance of grass AIT treatment with that of conventional grass subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) administered by physicians. Method: Nine hundred and ninety patients with grass pollen induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis who initiated immunotherapy in 2007 with either SCIT (Phleum pratense, 100 000 SQ-U/ml) or SQ-standardised AIT (Phleum pratense 75 000 SQ-T/2800 BAU) were included in the analyses. Patient and prescription data covering the period 2007- 2009 was extracted from the Prescribed Drug Registry, the National Board of Health and Welfare in Sweden. Data on patients treated and number of packs sold were used to calculate the compliance and persistence for each of the two products, for patients who started treatment in 2007. Compliance: calculated as the duration of treatment estimated from the number of packs or vials sold and used according to the pack leaflet (assuming 100% compliance), divided by the actual duration of treatment (the time estimated from the first to the last observed prescription, plus the use duration of the last pack or vial). Persistence: calculated as the percentage of patients who continued their treatment in 2009 with at least one treatment pack or vial in 2009. Result: Grass AIT treatment was started by 636 patients and grass SCIT treatment by 354 patients in 2007. The persistence of treatment in 2009 was 55% for grass AIT treatment and 57% for grass SCIT treatment. The estimated average duration of treatment was 2.34 years for grass AIT and 2.47 for grass SCIT at cut-off 31 December 2009. The average number of tablets used per patient during this period was 770. For grass SCIT treatment the average number of up-dosing kits used was 1.07 and the average number of maintenance vials was 3.26 (five injections per vial). This corresponded to a compliance of 90% for grass AIT and 82% for grass SCIT. Conclusion: The persistence of SQ-standardised grass AIT and grass SCIT treatments during the period 2007-2009 for Swedish patients was comparable. Compliance to treatment with SQ-standardised grass AIT and grass SCIT treatments were both high (≥80%) and comparable.

Method: All trials were randomised, doubleblind, placebo-controlled multi-centre trials. How to define 'curing allergy'? Results from a subcutaneous specific immunotherapy study using a high-dose hypoallergenic grass pollen preparation; Background: Specific immunotherapy is considered to be the only treatment with immanent ability to cure allergy due to modulation of the immune system. Up to now, an accepted definition of 'curing allergy' is lacking. We applied definitions according to the provisions stated in the Guideline on the Development of Products for Specific Immunotherapy using follow up data of a DBPC SCIT trial with a grass pollen allergoid. Method: The mentioned guideline roughly defines curing allergy to be the 'sustained absence of allergic symptoms in post treatment years'. We used three definitions for 'absence of allergic symptoms'. The most stringent definition A, considers cure of allergy as complete absence of symptoms without intake of any allergic medication during the whole analysis period of the diary phase. Definition B - nearest to the guideline wording - also assesses cure if no allergic symptoms are noted. But in contrast to definition A, intake of medication does not contradict a cure of allergy. Due to the fact that even healthy, non-allergic patients suffer from nasal or ocular symptoms sporadically, a more practically definition C specifies cure if one mild symptom (or respective medication) per day in mean is present. These definitions are applied to data of an investigation 3 years after end of treatment of a DBPC clinical trial. Result: Twenty-six patients suffering from allergic rhinoconjunctivitis at the beginning of double-blind treatment of the study could be evaluated 3 years after the end of the SCIT and compared to a control group of 13 patients who did not receive a SCIT. None of the non-treated patients can be considered as cured in any of the three definitions. In contrast, 6 (23%) and 7 (27%) patients of the former SCIT-group satisfy the very stringent definitions A and B, respectively. Twelve patients (46%) meet definition C which mimics the real life setting most exactly. Regarding this definition, statistically significant more patients of the former SCIT-group as compared to the control group have cured their allergy (P = 0.003). Conclusion: Three definitions for the claim 'Curing Allergy' were proposed and analyzed with real study data. A definition allowing for low level of symptoms seen also in non allergic patients is recommended since it considers the real life situation most relevantly. Compared to untreated patients significantly more patients treated with the high-dose hypoallergenic grass pollen allergoid satisfy this definition of 'Curing Allergy'.

Is intralymphatic specific immunotherapy with grass pollen allergen ready for clinical use?; Background: Allergen-specific immunotherapy is the only causative treatment for IgE-mediated allergic diseases, but it is time-consuming. Treatment with direct administration of allergen into a lymph node has been suggested to reduce the necessary administrations to three, compared to the fifty injections in standard subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT). This is the first randomized, double blind, placebocontrolled study with primary endpoints following the EMA-guidelines, in terms of safety and efficacy (seasonal combined symptom-medication scores) of intralymphatic injections of two different dosages of grass pollen-allergen. Secondary endpoints were VAS- and RQLQ-scores, SPT (Skin Prick Test), intracutaneous-test and immunological changes. Method: 45 patients (18-60 years) with a history of seasonal rhinoconjunctivitis, positive SPT and specific IgE to grass pollen were included. Exclusion criteria were pregnancy, other significant disease, bblockers or previous immunotherapy. The study included three arms. Group 6.: 6 weekly injections of allergen, group 3.: 3 allergen injections plus three placebo, and a placebo group: six placebo-injections. Each treatment containing 1000 SQ-U of Phleum pratense allergen extract (approximateley 0.25 lg of major allergen) or 0.1 ml of saline was injected into a lymph node in the groin guided by ultrasound. Result: No significant differences in the combined symptom and medication score (SMS) were found between groups when assessing the entire season. Additionally the 3· group experienced significantly higher SMS during peak season compared to placebo (0.52 vs 0.30, P = 0.015). Compared to the pre-treatment season VAS, RQLQ and SPT showed no clinical efficacy of intralymphatic immunotherapy. Specific IgG4 and IgE increased only in treated groups, and the intracutaneous test showed a significant improvement for the 6· compared to the placebo group. Systemic reactions were seen in two patients with severe conjunctival symptoms and axillary flare and itching in less than 30 min after allergen- injection. Additionally one experienced decreased peak flow. Conclusion: We found no clinical efficacy of intralymphatic injections compared to placebo. Thus with our design the intralymphatic treatment is not a viable competitor to SCIT, even when administering twice the number of injections used in former studies. Increasing the treatment dose cannot be advised since systemic reactions were seen in approximateley 10 percent of the patients.

Allergen immunotherapy for allergic respiratory diseases; Allergen specific immunotherapy involves the repeated administration of allergen products in order to induce clinical and immunologic tolerance to the offending allergen. Immunotherapy is the only etiology-based treatment that has the potential for disease modification, as reflected by longterm remission following its discontinuation and possibly prevention of disease progression and onset of new allergic sensitizations. Whereas subcutaneous immunotherapy is of proven value in allergic rhinitis and asthma there is a risk of untoward side effects including rarely anaphylaxis. Recently the sublingual route has emerged as an effective and safer alternative. Whereas the efficacy of SLIT in seasonal allergy is now welldocumented in adults and children, the available data for perennial allergies and asthma is less reliable and particularly lacking in children. This review evaluates the efficacy, safety and longterm benefits of SCIT and SLIT and highlights new findings regarding mechanisms, potential biomarkers and recent novel approaches for allergen immunotherapy. © 2012 Landes Bioscience.
Specific immunotherapy in grass pollen allergy; Since its description by Noon in 1911, desensitization, or allergen specific immunotherapy (SIT), has been largely used in respiratory allergic diseases treatment. It remains the only etiologic treatment for allergic diseases. The development of the sublingual route and new forms of medication, as an alternative to subcutaneous injection, has led to large scale clinical trials. Many of them had been performed with allergen tablets, particularly in the field of pollen allergy. These studies have confirmed that SIT is efficient in reducing all respiratory allergic symptoms. Data on long-term benefits and sustained efficacy after stopping treatment have also been published. These show an impact on natural history of allergic disease, in particular, a reduction in the risk of asthma in desensitized rhinitic subjects and in the acquisition of new sensitivities. The basic mechanisms of immunotherapy are becoming better understood and allow us to envisage improvements in this therapeutic method in the future. The sublingual route appears to be safer with a better safety profile. This may lead to an extension of allergen specific immunotherapy indications in patients with respiratory allergic diseases. © 2012 Landes Bioscience.

Analysis of allergen immunotherapy studies shows increased clinical efficacy in highly symptomatic patients; Background: The assessment of allergen immunotherapy (AIT) efficacy in the treatment for seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis (SAR) symptoms is challenging. Allergen immunotherapy differs from symptomatic therapy in that while symptomatic therapy treats patients after symptoms appear and aims to reduce symptoms, AIT is administered before symptoms are present and aims to prevent them. Thus, clinical studies of AIT can neither establish baseline symptom levels nor limit the enrolment of patients to those with the most severe symptoms. Allergen immunotherapy treatment effects are therefore diluted by patients with low symptoms for a particular pollen season. The objective of this analysis was to assess the effect possible to achieve with AIT in the groups of patients presenting the most severe allergic symptoms. Methods: Study centres were grouped into tertiles categorized according to symptom severity scores observed in the placebo patients in each centre (low, middle and high tertiles). The difference observed in the average score in each tertile in active vs placebo-treated patients was assessed. This allowed an estimation of the efficacy that could be achieved in patients from sites where symptoms were high during the pollen season. Results: An increased treatment effect was observed in the most severe patients and was independent of the study analysed and symptom score used. Conclusions: The use of a tertile approach to analyse efficacy in AIT in SAR clinical studies can give a more accurate assessment of potential clinical benefit. © 2011 John Wiley & Sons A/S.

Multiple-allergen and single-allergen immunotherapy strategies in polysensitized patients: Looking at the published evidence; RATIONALE: In allergen immunotherapy, there is debate as to whether polysensitized patients are best treated with many allergens simultaneously (a predominantly North American approach) or a single, clinically problematic allergen (a predominantly European approach). METHODS: We reviewed the literature on single- and multi-allergen allergen immunotherapy in polysensitized and monosensitized patients. RESULTS: In individuals seeking treatment for moderate-to-severe respiratory allergies, polysensitization is more prevalent (range: 50%- 80%) than monosensitization in both the USA and Europe. Hence, singleallergen preparations will almost certainly have been clinically tested in polysensitized patients. In robust, large-scale clinical trials of grass pollen SCIT and SLIT, polysensitized subjects benefited at least as much from single-allergen immunotherapy as monosensitized patients did. There were no obvious safety profile differences between polysensitized and monosensitized participants. A recent trial of single-allergen SLIT versus multiallergen SLIT in predominantly polysensitized patients concluded that the co-administration of multiple allergens may have interfered with the effectiveness of the single-allergen timothy extract. Other studies suggest that multi-allergen SCIT is less effective in polysensitized patients than single-allergen allergen immunotherapy is in monosensitized subjects and that higher allergen doses are needed in multi-allergen SCIT. CONCLUSIONS: According to an evidenced-based analysis, singleallergen preparations (grass pollen extracts) are clearly efficacious and safe in polysensitized participants. Sublingual and subcutaneous multi-allergen immunotherapy in polysensitized patients needs more supporting data in large clinical trials to validate it as a treatment option. More work is also required to determine whether single- and multi-allergen immunotherapy protocols elicit distinct immune responses in monosensitized and polysensitized subjects.
The risk of severe treatment related adverse events is significantly lower in children compared to adults when treated with standardized timothy grass allergy immunotherapy tablets: Post Hoc analysis of 7 clinical trials; Background: Allergy immunotherapy tablets (AIT) provides a safer and more convenient alternative to subcutaneous specific immunotherapy treatment. However, severe adverse events occur infrequently. These events are rare and therefore pooled safety data from 1 phase II/III and 6 phase III clinical trials (5 in adults, 2 in children (5-17 years)) with grass AIT (Grazax, Phleum pratense 75,000 SQ-T/2800 BAU, ALK, Denmark) were analysed. Method: All trials were randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multi-centre trials. Subjects suffered from grass pollen induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis with or without asthma, had positive skin prick test and specific IgE to Phleum pratense. Subjects received once-daily sublingual treatment with grass AIT or placebo for approximately 24 weeks. The 5 adult trials comprised 2095 treated subjects (AIT = 1060, placebo = 1035) and the 2 children trials comprised 597 treated subjects (AIT = 301, placebo = 296). Adverse events were assessed by the investigator as treatment- related (possible or probable) or unlikely related and for seriousness. Application site-related events were defined as adverse events in relation to the oral cavity. Results: In the adult trials, 71% of AIT-treated subjects reported treatmentrelated adverse events compared to 24% for placebo. In the children trials the corresponding numbers were 63% for AIT and 27% for placebo. Of the AITtreated subjects 2 children (0.7%) and 32 adults (3.0%) experienced severe treatment-related events. The odds for severe events was 4.7 times lower in children compared to adults (odds-ratio with 95% CI, 0.22 [0.025-0.85], P = 0.019). The odds for having severe related application site adverse events was 2.6 times lower in children compared to adults (odds-ratio with 95% CI, 0.39 [0.04-1.63], P = 0.27, not statistically significant). No serious treatment-related adverse events were reported. Conclusion: This pooled analysis of over 2000 subjects in 7 clinical trials shows that the risk of experiencing severe treatment-related adverse events was significantly lower in children compared to adults when treated with of Timothy grass allergy immunotherapy tablets. This analysis provides evidence that Timothy grass AIT is an important and safe immunotherapy treatment option in children with grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis.

Economic evaluation of grass tablets for immunotherapy (oralair) compared to placebo in adults and children in Italy; Background: Specific immunotherapy is based on the regular administration over time of a maintenance dose of allergen extracts to allergic patients in order to modify the immune response, thus achieving a decrease in symptoms/drug intake and an improvement in quality of life, possibly on the long-term. Grass pollen tablet, Oralair (Stallergenes, Antony Cedex, France), were developed and registered for rhinoconjunctivitis allergy induced by grass pollen. There is sufficient evidence for the clinical efficacy of the product, but pharmaco-economy data are lacking. Methods: An economic analysis, using a rescue medication adjusted score (AASS) was performed, based on the available registration trialsdto assess the magnitude of Oralair effect if patients had not taken any rescue medication. In the present study the results of an adult and a pediatric study are pooled together with economic data in order to perform a cost-effectiveness analysis from the third party payer perspective. Medical visits, diagnostic exams, skin prick test, and drugs were valorized in euros according to the National tariffs and the standard drug prices in the Italian setting. The estimated ROC also enabled us to quantify the effectiveness in terms of Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALY). A decision tree was structured in order to model the possible outcomes and costs, according to a low, moderate and high AASS in adults and pediatric patients. A probabilistic sensitivity analysis was finally conducted to test the robustness of the results as well as the consistency with an assumed cost effectiveness threshold of euros 30.000/QALY. Results: The results showed a relative difference of 1.84 in favor of the active treatment versus placebo in absolute value in adult study and of 1.64 in pediatric study. The results also show how the Oralair administration costs 1024 euro/QALY with high and moderate AASS. Including also the loss of productivity the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) in adults is 700 euro/QALY. The 95% of the simulation performed by sensitivity analysis shows an ICER below the threshold of 30.000 euro/QALY. Conclusions: In conclusion our results show that Oralair grass tablet is a cost effective strategy in adults and pediatric patients with moderate and severe AASS.

Compliance and persistence to grass immunotherapy treatment is comparable for allergy immunotherapy tablets and subcutaneous immunotherapy: A swedish registry study; Background: Allergy immunotherapy tablets (AITs) are administered by the patients in their homes and the medical compliance and persistence may therefore be poorer than for subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) administered by physicians. Methods: Two products for the treatment of grass pollen induced ARC were investigated: a SCIT treatment (Alutard SQ, Phleum pratense, 100,000 SQ-U/ mL) and an AIT treatment (Grazax, Phleum pratense 75,000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU), ALK, Denmark). Data on patients treated and number of packages sold were used to calculate the compliance and persistence for each of the 2 products, for patients who started treatment in 2007. Compliance: calculated as the duration of treatment estimated from the number of packages sold (assuming 100% compliance), divided by the actual duration of treatment (the time estimated from the first to the last observed prescription, plus the duration of the last package). Persistence: calculated as the percentage of patients who continued their treatment in 2009 with at least initiation of 1 treatment package or vial in 2009. Results: Grass AIT treatment was started by 636 patients and the grass SCIT treatment by 354 patients in 2007. This corresponded to a compliance of 90% for grass AIT and 82% for grass SCIT. Conclusions: Compliance to treatment for grass ait and grass scit treatments were both high (>80%) and comparable. The persistence of swedish patients was comparable for grass AIT and grass SCIT treatments during the period 2007 to 2009.

Conclusions: Fast updosed immunologically enhanced SCIT with an optimized allergen/adjuvant ratio induced significant immunological effects and had an acceptable safety profile. Clinical efficacy will be investigated in future clinical trials. © 2012 John Wiley & Sons A/S.

Impact of pollen exposure on the treatment effect of ragweed and grass immunotherapy tablets for seasonalallergic rhinoconjunctivitis: Preliminary findings; Background: The overall magnitude of response to treatment of allergy immunotherapy tablets (AIT) for seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis (ARC) is impacted by pollen exposure. This analysis compares the efficacy of individual and pooled grass AIT (2800 BAU) and ragweed AIT studies (12 Amb a 1-U) across multiple seasons with variable pollen counts. Methods:The response to treatment from 5 pivotal, placebo-controlled trials of grass AIT (n=1793) and from 2 pivotal, placebo-controlled trials of ragweedAIT (n=644)were characterized. For each trial, subjects took daily tablet treatment for at least 8 weeks prior to and during the specific pollen seasons. Rescue medications and symptoms were recorded in eDiaries daily. The total combined daily symptom and medication scores (TCS), daily symptom scores (DSS), and daily medication scores (DMS) were calculated during the entire pollen seasons. Pollen counts were collected during each trial. Results: Seasons with high peak pollen counts generally favored larger treatment effects. Average peak season pollen counts varied between 48 to 106 grains/m3 for grass pollen and from 193 to 227 grains/m3 for ragweed pollen. The average TCS among grass AIT treated subjects and among ragweed AIT treated subjects were reduced by 23% (p<0.001 for between-treatment differences) and 25% (p<0.001) relative to placebo, respectively. However, the effect of treatment varied from 10% to 41% dependent on the season and pollen exposure. In particular, the treatment impact on use of rescue medications increased during more robust pollen seasons, with DMS varying from 20% to 46%. The majority of AEs were mild, local, application- site reactions with no reports of anaphylactic shock. Conclusions: These results provide evidence of a consistent treatment effect of ragweed and grass AIT across multiple seasons. The treatment effect generally had a tendency of being larger in studies with higher pollen counts and longer seasons, but also has been replicated for shorter seasons and lower pollen counts.

The average Adjusted Symptom Score, a new primary efficacy end-point for specific allergen immunotherapy trials; Background In clinical trials, the efficacy of immunotherapy for allergic rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms is often evaluated with the average Rhinoconjunctivitis Total Symptom Score (ARTSS). Effective treatment is associated with a lower ARTSS vs. placebo but use of rescue medication to alleviate symptoms reduces the RTSS and decreases the mean difference between active treatment and placebo groups. Objective To develop and describe the average Adjusted Symptom Score (AdSS), a new end-point reflecting symptom severity and rescue medication use in allergic rhinoconjunctivitis trials. Methods To calculate the AdSS, the RTSS is adjusted as follows: if a patient takes rescue medication on day d, the day's AdSS (AdSSd) is defined as the value of RTSSd or AdSSd-1, whichever is higher. The AdSS on the following day (AdSSd+1) is defined as the value of RTSSd+1 or AdSSd, whichever is higher. The average of the daily AdSSs (during the season) was calculated post hoc for two trials investigating the efficacy of five-grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy tablets in adult and paediatric patients and compared with the ARTSS and three other outcome measures (the average Rescue Medication Score (ARMS), the ARTSS and the average Combined Score). Results The average AdSS clearly discriminated between active and placebo treatments and confirmed the original ARTSS results. Adjustment for rescue medication use decreased the observed placebo effect. Conclusion and Clinical Relevance The average AdSS can be a valuable alternative to the ARTSS as a primary efficacy end-point in grass pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis trials. By adjusting the RTSS for rescue medication use, the AdSS can estimate symptom severity and the treatment effect more accurately. The AdSS is now being tested prospectively in large clinical trials. © 2011 Blackwell Publishing Ltd.

Dosing and efficacy in specific immunotherapy; Allergen-specific immunotherapy is used to treat allergic rhinoconjuctivitis and asthma worldwide. The clinical efficacy of the most common routes, subcutaneous (SCIT) and sublingual (SLIT) immunotherapy, is documented for respiratory allergy by double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised clinical trials (DB PC RCT). However, dose-effect relationships are not available for all extracts. The 1998 WHO Consensus Report on Allergen Immunotherapy found SCIT ineffective at low doses, with high doses more likely to result in an unacceptably high level of systemic reactions. Recent large well-designed DB PC RCTs using SLIT grass pollen tablets have undergone phase II-III studies in adults with allergic rhinitis, yielding proper dose-response studies. These were analysed by the European Academy of Allergy and Clinical Immunology Immunotherapy Interest Group task force on dose effect. In general, low doses (5-7 μg of allergen Phl p 5 per day) are ineffective. Daily doses of 15-25 μg of the major allergen protein are required for significant clinical improvement measured by symptom scores. A higher dose (33-40 μg of Phl p 5 per day) was not more effective than 15-25 μg. Optimization of the allergen/adjuvant ratio may allow for lower allergen doses, increase the safety/efficacy profile and allow for shorter updosing. However, our analysis of the available studies concluded that every product requires its own dose-response relationship study. © 2011 John Wiley & Sons A/S.
Safety and tolerability of immunotherapy using various updosing schedules of a new SCIT product with an optimised allergen/aluminium hydroxide ratio; Allergen extracts for subcutaneous specific immunotherapy (SCIT) may be adsorbed to aluminium hydroxide for adjuvant effect and to delay allergen discharge. A product with an optimised allergen-to-aluminium hydroxide ratio enables a lower allergen dose and shorter introduction phase. The new therapeutic product Avanz (ALK, Denmark) has an optimised allergen-to-aluminium hydroxide ratio. A multicentre, randomised, phase II clinical trial evaluated the immunological effects and tolerability of two different five-step updosing schedules for Avanz in 400 patients with grass pollen-induced rhinoconjunctivitis with or without asthma, randomised into two groups. Group 1 were administered weekly, and group 2 were administered every 3 to 4 days. After updosing, patients received two maintenance injections after 2 and 4 weeks. In the updosing phase, local and systemic reactions were significantly more frequent in group 2 than group 1. In the maintenance phase, adverse reactions were less common in both groups. No generalised reactions with hypotension or fatal reactions occurred. An increase in allergen-specific immunoglobulin G 4 (IgG4) and IgE antibodies was established one week after the last injection. Avanz is a SCIT product with an optimised allergen-to-aluminium hydroxide ratio that enables a shorter updosing phase. We established an improved safety profile with weekly updosing compared with 3-4-day intervals. Clinical trials are needed to confirm clinical efficacy. © 2011 John Wiley & Sons A/S.

Efficacy of sublingual allergen immunotherapy tablets on individual symptom scores in adults with grass polleninduced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis; Background: Common symptoms of seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis include rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, sneezing, nasal, ocular pruritus and watery eyes. The 300IR five-grass pollen sublingual allergen immunotherapy (SLIT) tablet has shown to provide single-season symptom relief in grass-pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis patients. The present long-term study aimed to demonstrate the treatment's sustained efficacy. Method: 633 adults were included in a 3- year Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled phase III trial. Patients were randomized to placebo or 1 of 2 active groups, receiving each year pre and coseasonal treatment starting either 4 or 2 months prior to the pollen season. Four nasal and two ocular symptoms were scored daily on a scale ranging from 0 (no symptoms) to 3 (severe symptoms). Here is reported results from the secondary analysis on the 6 individual Average Rhinoconjunctivitis Symptom Scores (ARSSs) over the 3rd pollen season. Result: Over the 3rd pollen season, significant improvement was observed for all ARSSs. All nasal symptom scores were significantly lower versus placebo and as example for nasal congestion: the relative LS Means difference versus placebo were )42.9% (P = 0.0001) and )36.2% (P = 0.0011) in the 4 and 2 months pre and coseasonal treatment groups, respectively. The two ocular symptoms were also significantly improved compared with placebo giving respectively a relative LS Means difference versus placebo of )44.3% (P = 0.0014) and )47.4% (P = 0.0007) for ocular pruritus and )34.5% (P = 0.0002) and )34.0% (P = 0.0003) for watery eyes. These benefits were apparent in the first season and increased season after season during the 3 seasons of treatment. Conclusion: The sustained efficacy over a three-year period of 300IR 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet with a pre and coseasonal treatment was demonstrated. The treatment was effective on multiple allergic symptoms (including nasal congestion) of rhinoconjunctivitis.
In search of surrogate markers of sublingual allergen-specific immunotherapy efficacy; Background: Whereas large clinical trials have confirmed the efficacy of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) to treat respiratory allergies, biomarkers predicting clinical responses remain to be identified. Method: Herein, changes in 140 immune parameters were investigated in 82 patients in the course of a randomized doubleblind, placebo-controlled study conducted in an allergen challenge chamber. Protein profiling was performed in sera from 36 patients representative of 4 groups of patients i.e. active responders/ active non responders/ placebo responders and placebo non responders. Result: Treatment with a 5-grass-pollen tablet led to a 29% improvement versus placebo of the mean average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) at end point. The latter was documented in patients exhibiting distinct patterns of IgE sensitization against grass pollen allergens. No neosensitization was observed in the course of SLIT. Clinical responders were defined as the 25% of patients with the highest relative improvement in symptom score from baseline, with at least a 49% decrease of ARTSS after treatment. SLIT led to a decrease in TNF-αlpha production and a trend towards a higher expression of IFN-gamma in PBMCs, but with no link with clinical efficacy. No changes in basophil activation nor T-cell proliferation were observed. A higher expression of Treg markers and a lower expression of molecules associated with a Th1 or Th2 profile were seen for both active and placebo groups. Active responders were found to encompass both ''immunoreactive'' patients with strong specific IgG, IgE and IgG4 responses (possibly blocking antibodies), as well as ''non immunoreactive'' responders with no detectable antibody responses distinguishing them from placebo. Protein profiling conducted by 2DDiGE and mass spectrometry analyses in sera from 36 patients led to the identification of three potential predictive markers for SLIT efficacy, only found in the sera of active responders. These proteins are possibly involved in innate immunity. Conclusion: None of the conventional immune parameters tested can be used as biomarkers of efficacy. Further analyses conducted on larger cohorts of patients are on-going to validate the three candidate biomarkers predictive for SLIT efficacy.
Direct comparison between continuous and co-seasonal regimen for sublingual immunotherapy in children with grass allergy. A randomised controlled study; Background: Pre-seasonal, pre-coseasonal and continuous regimens of immunotherapy have been proposed, but their efficacy was never compared. We compared the clinical efficacy of a continuous and a coseasonal SLIT for grass allergy over 3 years. Methods: Children with rhinitis/asthma due to grass were randomised to SLIT given continuously (all year long) or coseasonally. The treatment started in October 2005 in the continuous SLIT group and in march 2006 in the coseasonal group Diary cards for clinical symptoms (from 0 = none to 3 = severe) and drug intake were recorded form march to june in 2005 (baseline), 2006 2007 and 2008. Specific IgE and IgG4 were evaluated every year. Results: Eighty children (age range 8-16) were randomised and 72 completed the study. In the first year, the symptom + medication score improved by 44% in the continuous group and by 20% in the coseasonal group (P = 0.04). Symptoms, chest symptoms and drug intake separately showed a greater decrease versus baseline in the continuous group. In the second year the global score decreased in both groups with no significant difference, whereas symptom score decreased more in the continuous group. In the 3rd year, there was no difference in clinical parameters between the two groups. Specific IgG4 were significantly higher versus baseline since the 1st year in the continuous group and since the 2nd in the coseasonal group. Conclusion: In grass pollen allergy the continuous regimen is more effective than the coseasonal in the first season, whereas in the subsequent years the two regimens are nearly equivalent.

Consistency of short-and long-term clinical trials results with 300 IR five-grass pollen tablets; Background: A total of 1539 patients with grass pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis were included in two short-term and one long-term European DBPC trials. The efficacy of once daily pre and coseasonal allergen immunotherapy with 300 IR five-grass pollen tablets was demonstrated with good safety profile, in adult and pediatric populations. Method: The treatment efficacy over the pollen period was assessed by the improvement in the Average Rhinoconjunctivitis Total Symptom Score (ARTSS) in the short-term studies and the improvement in the Average Adjusted Symptom Score (AAdSS, a score that integrates the symptoms and rescue medication use) in the long-term study. Post hoc analyses were performed on data from the short-term studies with the AAdSS. Individual symptom scores and safety were studied as secondary endpoints in all trials. Result: The adjusted mean improvements in the AAdSS versus placebo were 30.2% and 28.2% in the short-term adult and paediatric studies respectively. This improvement reached 34.5% over the 3rd pollen season of the long term adult study in patients who received a 4-month preand co-seasonal treatment scheme. Large improvement was also noted in all individual symptoms (especially nasal congestion and ocular symptoms) in adults and children. The majority of patients in active groups showed lower symptom scores from the first pollen season onwards. The treatment was well tolerated. Adverse events were mostly localised at site of administration and of mild-to-moderate in intensity. Conclusion: The efficacy and safety of a 300 IR five-grass pollen tablet in a pre and coseasonal treatment was demonstrated in two short-term adult and paediatric studies and in a long-term adult study. These results support the use of the 300 IR fivegrass pollen tablet in clinical practice in adults and children with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.

Considerable 6 years post treatment long-term effect of pre-seasonal subcutaneous specific immunotherapy (SCIT) with a high-dose hypoallergenic grass pollen preparation; Background: Pre-seasonal SCIT with a high-dose hypoallergenic 6-grass pollen preparation has previously been shown to be efficacious and safe in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (2002-2003). During the third year of active treatment (2004) continuous improvement was observed. Within the framework of a long-term follow-up survey we prospectively investigated efficacy, disease specific Quality of Life during the grass pollen season and skin prick test sensitivity in 2010 6 years after completion of SCIT. Method: 21 patients (6 males, 15 females, mean age of 36.8 years in 2002), who had been actively treated with 3 pre-seasonal courses of SCIT with Allergovit 6-Grasses were included (Full Analysis Set). Patients recorded their rhinoconjunctivitis and lower airways symptoms and their use of rescue medication, which by combination yielded a symptom-medication score (SMS). Rhinoconjunctivitis specific Quality of Life was assessed using a standardized questionnaire (RQLQ). The skin prick test (SPT) sensitivity to various seasonal and perennial allergens was assessed. Result: Grass pollen exposure in the 6 weeks observation period was similar in the gras pollen season of the last treatment year 2004 (925 grains/m3) and 6 years after the end of treatment in 2010 (1042 grains/ m3). The median AUC of the SMS, which had been largely improved during SCIT to 148.0 score points in 2004, remained comparably low (127.0 score points) in 2010. Six years after cessation of SCIT patients recorded 79% of days in the grass pollen season as 'well days' (days with a symptom score ≤4 and without use of rescue medication). In addition, disease-specific Quality of Life remained constantly high with a mean RQLQ score of 0.9 points in 2004 and 1.1 in 2010. Six years after the end of treatment 35% of patients did not show any new sesitization in the SPT. Conclusion: SCIT with the high-dose hypoallergenic 6-grass pollen preparation achieved a long-term effect on allergic symptom-medication score and Quality of Life in adults for at least six post treatment years. The results confirm the earlier report of long-term effects of this preparation in children for up to12 years post treatment.

Method: All trials included subjects with grass pollen AR with or without diagnosed seasonal asthma. Subjects with uncontrolled asthma were excluded. Safety data were pooled from five adult and two paediatric randomised, placebo-controlled trials with the SQ-standardised grass AIT (Grazax, phleum pratense 75 000 SQ-T/ 2800 BAU, ALK, Denmark), comprising 2096 adults (five phase II/III trials) and 598 children 5-17 years of age (Two phase III trials). Asthma-related adverse events (AEs) were captured both in the e-diary as asthma symptoms and recorded as AEs. The frequencies of events were compared between the active treatment and placebo groups in sub-groups of subjects with and without diagnosed asthma. The selected adverse events were: asthma, dyspnea, wheezing, cough, chest tightness or discomfort, and exercise-induced symptoms. Result: In adults diagnosed with asthma (n = 516) there were fewer reports of asthma-related AEs in the grass AIT group (59.6%) than in the placebo group (66.8%)
Gramole study: Obtaining, in routine clinical practice, the profile of in vitro allergic sensitisation of patients with seasonal allergic rhinitis and double in vivo sensitisation to olive and grass pollens; Background: Grass and olive tree pollens have widely overlapping pollination periods in Spain, therefore, the identification of the true etiological agent in patients sensitized to allergens causing cross-sensitization is very difficult if only skin-prick test (SPT) with the extracts currently available (mixture of proteins with presence of major and minor allergens) is used. The aim of the present study was to determine the sensitization pattern of grass pollen (Phl p 1 + 5) and olive tree pollen (Ole e 1) major allergens, detected by means of specific IgE in patients with seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR) and positive skin test (SPT) to both grass and olive pollens. Additionally, we evaluated how the knowledge of sensitization patterns against these allergens may influence on allergen immunotherapy (AIT) prescription. Method: Patients of both sexes, aged 5- 65 years, with diagnosis of SAR clinically associated to grass and olive pollinosis and double sensitization to these pollens, were recruited. Informed written consent was obtained. The primary endpoint of this study was the serum determination of specific- IgE levels to Ole e 1 and Phl p 1 + 5. These measurements permitted defining patterns of in vitro sensitization according to different cut-off points considered as positive (0.35 kU/l, 0.70 kU/l, 2 kU/l, 3.5 kU/l), based on Enzyme Allergosorbent Test classification. Investigators were asked to select the most appropriate AIT before and after diagnosis with recombinant allergen- specific IgE (Gramineae 100%, Gramineae and Olive or Olive 100%). Result: 1263 patients were recruited by 88 allergists. Double in vitro sensitization (Ole e 1 and Phl p 1 + 5) for a sIgE cutoff ≥ 0.35 kU/l (class I) was 71% [30% if the cut-off is set to > 3.5 kU/l (class III)]. Similarly, positives only to Phl p 1 + 5 ranged between 14% to 27% and positives only to Ole e 1 ranged between 12% and 17%. Once known the results of in vitro test, the allergists interviewed would change the composition of immunotherapy in 55% of patients with persistent and moderate-severe SAR. Conclusion: Diagnosis using recombinant allergens allows a more accurate diagnosis of patients multisensitized to pollens and, in some cases, knowledge of the results of this test may lead to a better adaptation of immunotherapy composition.
A phase I clinical trial with SCIT vaccines from timothy grass pollen extracts according to the new EMA guidelines; Background: There are only a few published studies covering phase I clinical trials of allergen immunotherapy and most of them belong to sublingual preparations. In June 2009 a new EMA Guideline concerning clinical development of products for specific immunotherapy for the treatment of allergic diseases came into force (CPMP/EWP/18504/2006) recommending that early studies should be done under a phase I format to test different doses to provide preliminary data on safety and tolerability with regard to the maximum tolerated dose and a suitable dose escalation scheme. Method: A single centre phase I randomised double blind placebo controlled study of subcutaneous immunotherapy in adult subjects (18 to 60 years) with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis ± asthma sensitised to Phleum pratense pollen was carried out. A total of 42 patients were enrolled. The principal variable of the study was the number and seriousness of both local and systemic adverse reactions. Secondary clinical end points included immunoglobulin determination: specific IgE, total IgG and IgG4 and dose-response prick test. Three different build up phase schedules were assayed, one involving six injections on a weekly basis (A), another one of eight injections (B) and a clustered administration of four double injections (C). Each group included 14 patients. Concentrations ranged from 10 to 1.000 TSU/ml. Result: Group A administrations gave rise to 26 local reactions and 4 systemic reactions (1 graded I and 3 graded II). Group B showed 35 local and 8 systemic (2 graded I and 1 graded II) reactions. Finally, group C patients experienced 20 local and 9 (5 graded I and 4 graded II) systemic reactions. None of the local events recorded were considered large reactions. Following injections with Timothy pollen extracts allergen specific IgE, IgG and IgG4 increased and skin reactivity to P. pratense was reduced. All schedules allowed reaching the dose of 500 TSU per injection that could be established as maximum tolerated dose. None of the patients discontinued treatment throughout the study. Conclusion: SCIT vaccines containing P. pratense depot extracts have shown a very good safety and tolerability profile and efficacy in terms of humoral and doseresponse prick test. Among the administration schedules used, Group A has shown a better tolerability and efficacy profile compared to Groups B and C.
Clinical efficacy of sublingual immunotherapy in seasonal allergic asthma; Background: The evaluate of efficacy of sublingual allergen specific immunotherapy (SLIT) in seasonal allergic asthma (SAA) have been performed predominantly by short-term studies in monosensitised patients. The aim of the study was to investigate short-term clinical effects of SLIT added to treatment with medical therapy (MT) in comparation to MT only in patients with SAA polisensitised to grass and ragweed pollen. Method: The prospective (randomized and controlled) study covered 17 adolescent and adult patients with mild to moderate severe SAA (with or without seasonal allergic rhinitis) induced by hypersensitivity to grass and ragweed pollen, indicated to SLIT. The experimental group was composed of 10 patients subjected to precoseasonal SLIT (antiallergic biologically standardized vaccines, sublingual drops) and MT, while seven adequate matched patients on MT only served as controls. The clinical efficacy of SLIT was evaluated by the symptom-drug (diary card) score (SDS) measurement, skin prick test (SPT) and non-specific bronchial hyperactivity (NBH) measurement (nonspecific bronchial provocation test by metacholine), before initiation of SLIT and 1 year later (in pollen season and after pollen season). Results: The SDS were significantly reduced in patients subjected to SLIT (P < 0.01) 1 year after the onset it. SPT to grass and ragweed pollen also was significantly reduced (P < 0.05) but NBH did not change. In patients receiving MT only, SDS was also significantly reduced (P < 0.01), but significantly higher (P < 0.05) from the value obtained in the experimental group. SPT and NBH remained unchanged and significantly higher (P < 0.05) then in experimental group. Conclusion: SLIT added to MT is clinically effective in patients with seasonal allergic asthma polisensitised to grass and ragweed pollen.
The effect of preseasonal grass pollen allergoid immunotherapy on basophil CD203c expression; Background: Short-term preseasonal immunotherapy has shown to be effective in pollinosis. To the best of our knowledge, there were no published studies that evaluate the impact of the allergoid immunotherapy on CD203c expression of basophils. We sought to assess the impact of preseasonal grass pollen allergoid immunotherapy on basophil CD203c expression and its clinical efficacy in patients with grass pollen related allergic rhinitis. Method: In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, 31 patients with allergic rhinitis sensitized only to pollens (confirmed by compatible history, and skin prick tests) received either grass pollen allergoids in a preseasonal immunotherapy protocol (n = 16) or placebo injections (n = 15). CD203c expressions were measured using flow cytometer after in-vitro stimulation with four different concentrations of grass pollen extract. The concentrations of the allergen extracts were expressed as the content of the major allergen Phl p 5. Basophil activation tests via CD203c were carried out immediately before and after the preseasonal immunotherapy/ placebo periods and at the peak pollen season. Symptom free days, medication free days and average visual analogue scores during the pollen season were compared to evaluate clinical efficacy. Result: The changes from baseline values (CD203c) were significantly different between the two groups after in-vitro stimulation with 4.5 10-4 μg/ml, 4.5 10-5 μg/ ml Phl p 5 (P < 0.05). The CD203c expressing activated basophil percentages after in-vitro stimulation with 4.5 10-4 μg/ ml, 4.5 10-5 μg/ml Phl p 5 significantly decreased compared to baseline in the immunotherapy group (P < 0.025). There were no significant differences in the CD203c expressing activated basophil percentages compared to baseline in the placebo group (P > 0.025). Symptom free days were significantly higher and average visual analogue scores were significantly lower in the immunotherapy group (P < 0.05). Medication free days were similar between the two groups (P > 0.05). Conclusion: This study indicates that preseasonal short course allergoid immunotherapy is an effective method in reducing symptoms of grass pollen related allergic rhinitis. Furthermore, a suppressive effect of the administered immunotherapy protocol was detected on the CD203c expression of activated basophils.
Specific immunotherapy improves the clinical response in patients with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis; Background: Specific immunotherapy (SIT) has a significant role in the treatment of allergic rhinitis and allergic conjunctivitis. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of specific immunotherapy on grasspollen induced rhino-conjunctivitis. Methods: We have evaluated the effect of standard regiment of SIT on the pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Twenty-six patients (age range 18-44 years) with positive history for more than 2 years and skin-prick test ≥ 5 mm underwent conjunctival provocation tests before and after 1 year of SIT. Clinical severity of nasal and conjunctival symptoms during the season was assessed by 4-point arbitrary rating scale from 0 to 3. Conjunctival provocation were done out of the season until allergic symptoms occurred achieving the allergen threshold dose (ATD). Results: After 1 year of SIT we found reduction in clinical symptoms of allergic conjunctivitis (burning, itching, lacrimation and hyperemia) P < 0.05 as well as reduction in clinical symptoms of allergic rhinitis (secretion, irritation, itching and nasal blockade) P < 0.01. Significantly higher allergen doses in provocation test (out of season) were tolerated after 1 year of performed SIT, reaching new ATD. Conclusions: Grass pollen SIT reduces clinical symptoms of allergic rhinoconjunctivitis and modifies the inflammatory response after specific allergen challenge.
Noticeable placebo response in clinical studies investigating efficacy of different preparations for subcutaneous specific immunotherapy; Background: Randomised, double-blind, placebo controlled (RDBPC) studies are currently the recommended standard of clinical trials. The outcome of these trials is affected by the placebo response which is driven by different mechanisms and influenced by a variety of factors e.g. invasiveness and duration of therapy or patient's attitude of expectation. Only clinical trials including a baseline exposure period provide the possibility to precisely investigate this effect in SIT. In past studies, only to a lesser extent baseline assessments were included. Methods: We analysed five randomised, double-blind, placebo controlled clinical trials including a baseline period, designed to assess efficacy and safety of SCIT in patients with allergic rhinitis (AR), allergic to grass pollen, birch pollen or mites, using the full analysis sets (FAS). In a total of 415 placebo treated patients the median change relative to baseline of the area under the curve (AUC) of the symptom medication score (SMS) after 2 years of placebo therapy was calculated. Evaluation periods covered 21 days for birch pollen, 42 days for grass pollen as well as 28 days for house dust mite (HDM) allergy. To obviate the possibility that different pollen exposure during the seasons influenced the results, the AUCs of birch and grass pollen grains/m3 during the evaluation periods were checked. Results: Birch pollen allergic placebo treated patients with AR (n = 216) demonstrated an improvement of the AUC of median SMS of 21.5%, grass pollen allergic placebo treated patients (n = 87) an improvement of 22.5%. Patients belonging to the placebo group with HDM allergy (n = 112) displayed an even exceeded improvement by 35.5% of their SMS compared to baseline. Pollen counts of the seasonal allergens were comparable for the analysed periods in 2 years. Conclusion: The results of different RDBPC clinical trials with a baseline period showed that the influence of subcutaneous placebo therapy is in the range of 22- 36% in SIT studies. Further investigations have to show if diverse application routes e.g. the sublingual route the placebo response to the same extent. .
Treatment with SQ-standardised grass allergy immunotherapy tablet impacted the number of days with low quality of life; Background: The quality of life of patients with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis is often impaired due to symptoms such as nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea, frequently resulting in sleep disruption. Purpose: to investigate how the number of days with severe symptoms (severe days) impacts the rhinoconjunctivitis quality of life and how the treatment with a grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT) impacts the frequency of severe days. Methods: Data from a multicentre, doubleblind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial of 5 years duration (3 years daily treatment and 2 years follow-up) with the grass AIT (Grazax, phleum pratense 75 000 SQ-T/ 2800 BAU, ALK, Denmark), were used. Six rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms (four nose and two eye) rated on a 4-point scale from 0 (no symptoms) to 3 (severe symptoms) were recorded on a daily basis. Quality of life was assessed with the Junipers rhinoconjunctivitis quality of life questionnaire (RQLQ) on a weekly basis in terms of seven domains each rated on a 7-point scale from 0 (not troubled/none of the time) to 6 (extremely troubled/all of the time). Post-hoc, the numbers of weekly (Table presented) severe days in at least one of the six symptom categories were merged with the RQLQ replies the same week (12324 data points) and analysed, using cubic B-splines and logistic regression. Results: The RQLQ score increased (=lower quality of life) with the number of weekly severe days. For example, the RQLQ score was 3.7 times higher for subjects with four or more weekly severe days (mean score: 2.93) than for subjects with no weekly severe days (mean score: 0. 79), Table 1. Treatment with grass AIT significantly reduced the odds of having severe days relative to placebo, P < 0.001, Table 1. The odds-ratio for grass AIT versus placebo for having severe days decreased with the number of weekly severe days. For example, the odds of having four or more weekly severe days were three times lower (odds-ratio = 0.3) in the group treated with grass AIT. Conclusion: Treatment with grass AIT significantly reduced the odds of having days with severe symptoms. Days with severe symptoms had a negative impact on the quality of life.

Meta-analysis supports that the efficacy of grass allergy immunotherapy tablets is comparable to subcutaneous immunotherapy; Background: Subcutaneous (SCIT) andsublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) havebeen shown to be effective in the treatmentof allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Allergen-Specific Immunotherapy: Which Outcome Measures are Useful in Monitoring Clinical Trials?; Various clinical outcome measures are commonly applied in clinical trials on specific immunotherapy for allergic rhinoconjunctivitis with or without asthma to provide evidence of its clinical efficacy. These "primary endpoints" measure clinical symptoms as well as the use for concomitant medication. "Secondary outcome endpoints" are represented by health-related quality of life (HRQoL), "well-days," provocation-tests, in vitro tests and others. This article reviews different methods assessing the clinical outcome of trials on both subcutaneous and sublingual immunotherapy, and highlights potential advantages and drawbacks of each method. © 2011 Elsevier Inc.
