Medication persistence with long-term, specific grass pollen immunotherapy measured by prescription renewal rates; Objective: We assessed medication persistence using prescription renewal rates for grass pollen specific immunotherapy (SIT) in a representative population of patients in Germany to evaluate whether the perception of superior persistence for the subcutaneous route compared to the sublingual route could be confirmed in clinical practice. Methods: Individual prescriptions for allergen immunotherapy were extracted from a national prescription database (INSIGHT Health) and followed over 3 years on a per-patient basis. However, patients' medical history and treatment schedules were not available for analysis. Products were identified by the national drug code (PZN number) and grouped to either subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) with natural extract injections, SCIT with modified allergens (allergoids) or sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) with natural pollen extract solutions. Persistence was defined as at least one prescription of the individual drug in the respective years. Results: A total of 1409 patients started SIT in 2005 (112, 695, and 602 for natural extract SLIT, natural extract SCIT, and allergoid SCIT, respectively). In 2006, 71%, 55%, and 59% of those patients had at least one renewal prescription of natural extract SLIT, natural extract SCIT, and allergoid SCIT, respectively, as well as 51%, 34%, and 39% in 2007. In both years, persistence with natural extract SLIT was significantly higher than with natural extract SCIT (p = 0.0015 for 2006, p = 0.0003 for 2007) and allergoid SCIT (p = 0.0152 for 2006, p = 0.0111 for 2007). There were no significant differences between the two SCIT groups. Conclusion: Medication persistence with grass pollen SIT in a representative sample of patients in Germany was similar to published medication persistence in asthma and COPD patients. The sublingual application route shows significantly better persistency than the subcutaneous route with native allergens or allergoids. © 2011 Informa UK Ltd All rights reserved.
Sublingual allergen-specific immunotherapy adjuvanted with monophosphoryl lipid A: A phase I/IIa study; Background: Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) allergy vaccines have an excellent safety profile, but opinions vary on their efficacy, and treatment regimens are often lengthy. This study assessed the effects of the Toll-like receptor 4 agonist monophosphoryl lipid A (MPL®) on safety/tolerability and clinical and immunological efficacy when combined with grass pollen SLIT formulations in treating patients with seasonal allergic rhinitis. This is the first reported study of adjuvanted SLIT. Methods: In this double-blind placebo-controlled phase I/IIa study, 80 grass pollen-sensitive subjects were randomized into 4 groups of 20 subjects to receive daily treatment for 8 weeks. Sixteen patients per group received SLIT and 4 received placebo. The formulation given to each group varied with respect to grass pollen extract and MPL content. Grass allergen nasal challenge tests (NCTs) were performed prior to dosing and in weeks 4 and 10. Grass pollen-specific immunoglobulin G (IgG) and IgE antibodies were measured at baseline and prior to dosing in weeks 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10. Results: Local and systemic adverse events were generally comparable for patients who received active treatment and placebo. Patients in the 2 groups given SLIT containing the highest amount of MPL experienced the highest proportion of negative NCTs after 10 weeks (47 and 44%, vs. 20% with placebo). These patients also showed earlier median increases in specific IgG and smaller increases in IgE levels than those receiving other formulations. Conclusions: These results suggest that SLIT preparations containing MPL are well tolerated and alter the immunological response to grass antigens after 3 weeks of exposure, with an associated suppression of nasal challenge responses. Long-term tolerance after allergen immunotherapy is accompanied by selective persistence of blocking antibodies; Background: Grass pollen immunotherapy for allergic rhinitis is a disease-modifying treatment that results in long-term clinical tolerance lasting years after treatment discontinuation. Active treatment is associated with generation of inhibitory grass pollen-specific IgG antibodies capable of blocking allergen-IgE interactions. Objectives: We sought to investigate the involvement of IgG-associated inhibitory antibodies with long-term clinical tolerance after discontinuation of grass pollen immunotherapy. Methods: We conducted a 4-year study in which patients who had moderate-to-severe allergic rhinitis underwent a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled discontinuation of subcutaneous grass pollen immunotherapy. All subjects received grass pollen immunotherapy injections for 2 years (n = 13), followed by a further 2 years of either active (n = 7) or placebo (n = 6) injections. Clinical outcomes included seasonal symptoms and use of rescue medication. Serum specimens were collected at baseline and after 2 and 4 years for quantification of allergen-specific IgG antibodies. Sera were also tested for IgG-dependent inhibitory bioactivity against IgE-allergen binding in cellular assays by using flow cytometry and confocal microscopy to detect binding of IgE-grass pollen allergen complexes to B cells. Results: Clinical improvement was maintained after 2 years of discontinuation. Although immunotherapy-induced grass pollen-specific IgG1 and IgG4 levels decreased to near-preimmunotherapy levels during discontinuation, inhibitory bioactivity of allergen-specific IgG antibodies was maintained unchanged. Conclusion: Grass pollen immunotherapy induces a subpopulation of allergen-specific IgG antibodies with potent inhibitory activity against IgE that persists after treatment discontinuation and that could account for long-term clinical tolerance. © 2010 American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology.

Consistency of clinical results throughout short-term and long-term studies with sublingual 300IR 5-grass pollen tablets; RATIONALE: 1533 patients were included in 2 short-term (adults and children) and in a long term (3-year treatment in adults) DBPC trials in Europe, assessing the once-daily pre-coseasonal allergen immunotherapy with 300IR 5-grass pollen tablets. Those studies demonstrated the safety and efficacy in adults and children with grass pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. METHODS: The treatment efficacy was assessed by the improvement of the RTSS in the short-term studies and the improvement of the Average Adjusted Symptom Score (AAdSS) in the long-term study during the pollen period. Adverse events were mostly local and mild-to-moderate in intensity. CONCLUSIONS: The 300IR 5-grass pollen tablet efficacy and safety was demonstrated in short-term adult, pediatric and in a long-term adult studies. Allergy immunotherapy tablet: Grazax® for the treatment of grass pollen allergy; Immunotherapy is the only treatment for allergy that alters the natural course of this disease. Sublingual immunotherapy has been developed to make immunotherapy more suitable for allergic patients. In the largest clinical program ever conducted with grass allergen-specific immunotherapy, over 2000 adults and more than 500 children have been exposed to Grazax® (ALK-Abello A/S, Hoersholm, Denmark). Grazax is an oral lyophilisate tablet (allergy immunotherapy tablet [AIT]) for sublingual administration, containing 75,000 standardized quality tablet units of allergen extract of grass pollen (Phleum pratense). Grazax is indicated for treatment of grass pollen-induced rhinitis and conjunctivitis in adult and pediatric patients. Results from the GT-08 trial (first, second and third treatment years) showed a reduction of 31, 36 and 29%, respectively, in symptom scores and a reduction of 38, 45 and 40% of medication scores, respectively, compared with placebo. Subjects treated with Grazax also had an increased number of well days and a relevant improvement in quality of life. More subjects experienced excellent and complete rhinoconjunctivitis control in comparison with patients treated with symptomatic medications only. Grazax treatment is also associated with a sustained and relevant increase of specific IgG4. This increase is also observed after stopping AIT treatment. The most common adverse events related to Grazax treatment are local reactions, such as oral itch, edema of the mouth, ear pruritus, throat irritation and sneezing. Clinical efficacy of Grazax is observed also after 1 and 2 years of follow-up after stopping the AIT treatment. Grazax is efficacious and safe for treatment of grass-pollen rhinoconjunctivitis in both adults and children. Grazax is the first AIT showing a disease-modifying effect on grass pollen-induced allergic rhinoconjuctivitis. © 2011 Expert Reviews Ltd.
Efficacy and safety of timothy grass allergy immunotherapy tablets in North American children and adolescents; Background: Allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT) treatment might be a safe and convenient form of specific immunotherapy but it has not been investigated in North American children and adolescents. Treatment lasted at least 8 weeks before the grass pollen season (GPS), and continued until the season finished. Specific immunoglobulin (Ig) G4, IgE, and IgE-blocking factor to Phleum pratense were measured at the beginning of the trial and at different intervals during treatment. Immediate and delayed skin tests with P pratense were also performed. Safety endpoints were defi ned in terms of adverse events reported. Results: A total of 75 patients completed the trial (50 active and 25 placebo). P pratense IgG4, IgE, and IgE-blocking factor in actively treated patients increased significantly from baseline to the start of the GPS compared to placebo (P>.001, P=.017, and P=.005, respectively) The immediate cutaneous response was reduced during therapy in actively treated subjects, whereas placebo-treated subjects showed a decrease only after the start of the GPS. The delayed response to the intradermal test in grass AIT-treated subjects diminished, although not in a significantly different way from the placebo-treated subjects. Conclusion: Treatment with grass AIT for grass pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis induces immunological changes after only 1 month of treatment. © 2010 Esmon Publicidad.

Efficacy and safety of grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT) in a North American pediatric population; Background: A number of immunological changes have been previously reported in subjects undergoing specific immunotherapy, particularly changes in allergen specific antibody responses. A phase 3, randomized trial was conducted to investigate the efficacy and tolerability of a new grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT) and its effects on IgG4 levels and IgE blocking factor in North American children. Methods: IRB approval was obtained at all sites and written informed consent obtained from subjects/legal guardians. 345 children (5-17 yrs) with grass pollen-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis were randomized 1:1 to once-daily 2800 BAU grass AIT (oral lyophilisate, Phleum pratense) or placebo (PBO) beginning approximately 16 weeks before and continuing through the 2009 grass pollen season (GPS). The primary efficacy endpoint was the total combined daily symptom and medication score (TCS). Secondary endpoints were daily symptom score (DSS), daily medication score (DMS), and the Pediatric or Adolescent Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaires (RQLQ). Specific IgG4 levels and IgE-blocking factor were measured before, during, and at the end of GPS. Safety was assessed by adverse events (AEs). Results: The mean GPS lasted 43 days (mean grass pollen count 28 grains/m3). 89% of subjects were multisensitized. AIT treatment yielded significant improvements relative to PBO in TCS (26%, P=0.001), DSS (25%, P=0.004), DMS (66%, P=0.006), and RQLQ (18%, P=0.028). The effect of grassAIT on IgG4 levels was significantly greater compared with PBO at peak season (P<0.001) and increased through the end of GPS (P<0.001). Similarly, the effect of grass AIT on IgE blocking factor was significantly greater compared with PBO at peak season (P<0.001) and was sustained through the end of GPS. The majority of treatment-related AEs were local, application site reactions. Conclusions: We report the first successful phase III pediatric grass AIT trial in North America. Once-daily administration of grass AIT is effective and well-tolerated, representing a new therapeutic modality for children with grass pollen-induced allergy. The effect of treatment on the immune system was confirmed by the changes in immunologic parameters, specifically increases in specific IgG4 and IgE blocking factor.

Assessment of sustained efficacy and safety of a 300IR 5-grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy tablet (SLIT) in adults with grass pollen induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis during a 3-year treatment study; Background: In single-season clinical trials, once-daily pre-coseasonal treatment with a 300IR 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet was shown to be safe and effective in adults and children. The aim of this study was to evaluate the sustained efficacy and safety of pre-coseasonal treatment with 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet in adults with grass pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Methods: 633 patients aged between 18 and 51 years were included in a DBPC, international, multi-centre Phase III trial to evaluate the sustained efficacy and safety of the 300IR 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet over 3 consecutive seasons. Patients were randomized to a placebo and 2 active groups, receiving either 4 or 2 months of pre-seasonal treatment and co-seasonal treatment. Use of rescue medication was permitted. The primary efficacy endpoint was the Average Adjusted Symptom Score (AAdSS, a score that integrates the symptoms and rescue medication use) over the 3rd pollen season. Results: 457 patients completed 3 consecutive seasons (2007, 2008 and 2009). Preliminary results of the 3rd pollen period showed a meanAAdSS±SD of 3.51±3.68 and 3.39±3.23 for the 4 and 2 months pre-seasonal treatment groups respectively, compared with 5.28±3.95 in placebo group. The efficacy of 300IR 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet seems to increase at every season, reaching a meanAAdSS improvement vs. placebo of 34% (median = 48%) in season 3 (4-month pre-seasonal treatment group). In this group, the mean AAdSS±SD was 3.79±3.95 in monosensitized patients and 3.31±3.49 in polysensitized patients. The treatment effect seemed to appear at lower pollen levels in the 2nd and 3rd seasons (booster effect). Treatment-related adverse events were mostly transient and mild to moderate in intensity, and their number decreased in the 2nd and 3rd treatment seasons. Conclusion: Three years of pre-coseasonal treatment with a 300IR 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet showed a sustained effect with statistical and clinically significant improvement of rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms in adults and a booster effect was observed. Efficacy was good in mono and in polysensitized patients. A potentially disease-modifying effect is now being investigated by discontinuing the SLIT and scoring the patients' symptoms for 2 additional seasons.
Efficacy and safety of timothy grass allergy immunotherapy tablet in North American adults; Background: Until now, the efficacy of grass sublingual immunotherapy has not been demonstrated in North America. This phase III trial investigated the efficacy and safety of daily administration of grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT) (oral lyophilisate, Phleum pratense, 2800 BAU) in allergic rhinocon-junctivitis (AR) subjects with or without asthma. Methods: 439 adults with Timothy grass pollen-induced AR were randomized 1:1 to once-daily grass AIT or placebo for approximately 16 weeks before and during the 2009 grass pollen season (GPS). Subjects used daily e-diaries to record AR symptoms from randomization through the end of the study. The use of symptomatic medications was also recorded in the e-diary during the GPS. The primary efficacy endpoint comprised the average total combined daily symptom and medication score (TCS) during the entire GPS. Key secondary endpoints were individual daily symptom score (DSS), daily medication score (DMS), and Rhinocon-junctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire (RQLQ[S]) with standardized activities. Immunologic endpoints included specific IgG4 and IgE-blocking factor. Safety was assessed by monitoring adverse events (AEs). IRB approval was obtained for all sites, and each subject provided written informed consent. Results: 85% of the subjects were multisensitized. The grass AIT group showed a mean 20% improvement in TCS compared with the placebo group (P=0.005). Similar positive outcomes in the AIT group relative to placebo were demonstrated for the DSS (18%, P=0.015), DMS (26%, P=0.084), and RQLQ(S) (17%, P=0.022). In the grass AIT group, significant increases in IgG4 and IgE blocking factor were observed at peak and end of GPS compared with placebo (P<0.001). The majority of AEs were mild local application site reactions that were transient in nature, with no treatment-related serious AEs in active subjects, one treatment-related serious AE in a placebo subject, and no reports of anaphylactic shock. Conclusions: Grass AIT is effective in a predominantly multisensitized North American adult population with Timothy grass pollen-induced AR. Once-daily administration of grass AIT was well tolerated and will provide a new therapeutic modality for patients with Timothy and related grass pollen-induced allergy.
Carbamylated monoid allergoids as a new therapeutic option for sublingual immunotherapy of mite- and grass-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis - A systematic review of published trials using Lais® tablets; Lais® allergoid tablets contain allergens, which are modified by carbamylation. Due to their modified chemical structure they are suitable for sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT). Based on their small molecule size of 12-40 kDa, they can be absorbed easily via the oral mucosa. In this review, the efficacy of SLIT with carbamylated monoid allergoid tablets on the treatment of grass pollen- and mite-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis was studied on the basis of symptom score and medication score improvement. Following a selective internet and databank search, six trials - in part also placebo-controlled - on the treatment of grass pollen- (n = 266) and mite-induced (n = 241) allergic rhinoconjunctivitis were suitable for conclusions regarding the clinical efficacy of allergoid tablets. The primary endpoints in these trials were the decrease in the need for antiall ergic medication and/or the reduction in the occurrence of rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms. Following data concerning symptoms and medication recorded in patient diaries, conclusions could be made about the effectiveness and tolerance of Lais® tablets. The average improvement of the symptom score for three trials on the treatment of grass pollen all ergy was 34% in comparison to improvement under placebo. For the treatment of mite-induced rhinoconjunctivitis, an average symptom score improvement of 22% became apparent compared to the placebo or control group. The intake of symptomatic PRN medication under therapy with allergoid tablets declined during the course of therapy. Under treatment of grass pollen allergy, the medication score improved by an average of 49% and by 24% in the treatment of mite-induced rhinoconjunctivitis as opposed to placebo or control. Only few side effects have been documented in trials and predominantly local effects have been observed. Severe systemic side effects did not occur. On the basis of the trial results summarized in this review, it can be suggested that SLIT with Lais® sublingual tablets is an effective and well-tolerated form of treatment.

Due to their modified chemical structure, they are suitable for sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) (13, 16, 17, 24). Based on their small molecule size of 12 to 40 kDa, they can be easily absorbed via the oral mucosa (1). The primary endpoints in these trials were decreases in the need for allergy medications and/or reductions in the occurrence of rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms. Data was recorded from patient diaries regarding their symptoms and medications used and conclusions were then drawn about the effectiveness of and tolerance to Lais® tablets. The average improvement in symptom score in three trials of grass pollen allergy treatment was 34% in comparison to the placebo group. The treatment of dust mite-induced rhinoconjunctivitis produced an average symptom score improvement of 22% compared to the placebo or control groups. The intake of symptomatic PRN medication during allergoid tablet therapy declined. Treatment of grass pollen allergies and dust mite-induced rhinoconjunctivitis showed an average medication score improvement of 49% and 24%, respectively. Few side effects were documented in the trials and predominantly local effects were observed. Severe systemic side effects did not occur. On the basis of the trial results summarized in this review, we suggest that SLIT using Lais® sublingual tablets is an effective and well-tolerated form of treatment.
Five-grass pollen 300IR SLIT tablets: Efficacy and safety in children and adolescents; The efficacy and safety of five-grass pollen 300IR sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) tablets (Stallergènes SA, France) have previously been demonstrated in paediatric patients. This report presents additional data concerning efficacy at pollen peak, efficacy and safety according to age, nasal and ocular symptoms, use of rescue medication, satisfaction with treatment and compliance. Children (5-11 yr) and adolescents (12-17 yr) with grass pollen-allergic rhinoconjunctivitis were included in a multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study and received either a 300IR five-grass pollen tablet or placebo daily in a pre- (4 months) and co-seasonal protocol. The severity of six symptoms (sneezing, rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion, nasal and ocular pruritis, and tearing) was scored, and rescue medication use was recorded daily during the pollen season. Patient satisfaction was recorded at the season end. A total of 161 children and 117 adolescents were evaluated (n = 267). 300IR SLIT was effective over the whole season (p = 0.0010) and at the pollen peak (p = 0.0009). The adjusted mean difference between 300IR and placebo groups was significant for both nasal (p = 0.0183) and ocular (p < 0.0001) symptoms. Rescue medication use was statistically lower in the SLIT group during the pollen season and at the pollen peak (both p < 0.05). More patients in the SLIT group were satisfied with their treatment compared to placebo (83.2% vs. 68.1%, p = 0.0030), and compliance was high (SLIT 93.9% of patients were compliant, placebo 94.8% of patients were compliant). SLIT was well tolerated by children and adolescents. 300IR five-grass pollen tablets are effective and safe during the pollen season and at the pollen peak in children and adolescents with grass pollen rhinoconjunctivitis. © 2010 John Wiley & Sons AS.
The biological potency of different extracts for sublingual immunotherapy assessed by skin prick tests; The standardization of allergen extracts is of primary relevance to the clinical efficacy. Biological standardization procedures are widely used in the commercial production of vaccines. We tested, in grass-allergic patients, the potency of three different grass extracts for sublingual immunotherapy by means of skin prick tests. Specific IgE against Phl p 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 11 and 12 were also assayed. Allerslit® and Sublivac® were directly applied as skin test. Grazax®, was prepared by dissolving two tablets in 2mL saline. Thirty-three subjects (mean age 38.8) were studied. The skin response was significantly different among extracts, decreasing from Allerslit to Grazax (t test <0.01), but all the extract produced a skin response greater than histamine. All the subjects had specific IgE to Phl p 1 and Phl p 4 but 24% did not have specific IgE to Phl p 5. In those subjects the skin response to the three extracts did not differ from that of Phl p 5-positive subjects. Our findings confirm that there is a variability in the biological potency among different extracts. In addition, the standardization of grass extracts based on Phl p 5 only, may be insufficient in some cases.
Subcutaneous immunotherapy with a preparation with optimised allergen aluminium hydroxide ratio: A randomised parallel-group clinical trial investigating safety and tolerability; Background: For subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) allergens usually are adsorbed to aluminium hydroxide (alum) for slow allergen release (depot effect). In addition alum also acts as an adjuvant that enhances the immunological effect. Therefore, a SCIT product with an optimised allergen/alum ratio allows for reducing the maximum dose applied for maintenance therapy and shorter up-dosing schedules. In a clinical trial safety and tolerability profile of a product with an optimised allergen/alum ratio has been investigated. Methods: In a randomised, controlled, parallel-group trial patients with rhinoconjunctivitis with/without asthma induced by grass pollen were treated with a SCIT depot preparation (four grasses and rye, AVANZ, ALK-Abello, Hørsholm, Denmark) containing 15% of the allergen content and 50% of the alum content compared with the widely used ALK allergen product for SCIT (Alutard SQ, ALK-Abelló, Hørsholm, Denmark). Therapy was initiated utilising an up-dosing phase with five injections (300, 600, 3000, 6000, 15 000 SQ+) with weekly intervals in group 1 and 3-4 days intervals in group 2 and was continued by two maintenance injections of 15 000 SQ+ with 14 and 28 days intervals. Results: In total 400 patients were treated (group 1: 201, group 2: 199) with the five injection up-dosing schedule. The trial was completed according to the injection schedule by 358 patients (group 1: 185, group 2: 173). Fewer local and systemic reactions were observed during up-dosing with one week intervals (group 1) compared with 3-4 days intervals (group 2). Local reactions were observed in group 1 in 68/201 patients (33.8%) and 93/199 (46.7%) patients in group 2. Delayed systemic reactions (1 h after the injection or later) occurred in 41/201 (20.4%) patients in group 1 and 63/199 (31.7%) patients in group 2 predominantly as rhinoconjunctivits or urticaria. The frequency of local and systemic reactions was much lower for the two maintenance injections in both treatment groups. Conclusion: Using a five injections up-dosing schedule a SCIT product with an optimised allergen/adjuvant ratio (AVANZ) was found to be well tolerated. Fewer local and systemic reactions were observed for up-dosing with injection intervals of 1 week compared with 3-4 days injection intervals.

Safety of sublingual immunotherapy for treatment of patients with severe asthma; Introduction: Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) has been established as an effective treatment for allergic rhinoconjunctivitis in adults, with fewer reported systemic adverse reactions than subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT). Definitive evidence for a benefit of SLIT in the treatment asthma is emerging. Currently patients with the most severe asthma (FEV1 < 70% predicted) are excluded from receiving immunotherapy (IMT) in trials and clinical practice guidelines. To date, no data has been published regarding the safety of SLIT in these patients. We describe a series of nine patients with postbronchodilator FEV1 of between 30 and 66% predicted who have received SLIT for several indications. Methods: Nine patients receiving SLIT with an FEV1 < 70% predicted prior to starting IMT were identified from pharmacy, hospital and departmental databases at three sites. There were five female and four male patients identified, with ages ranging from 33 to 65 years. Allergens used included house dust mite (HDM) only (five patients), HDM and grass pollen (three patients), and HDM, grass pollen and cat dander (one patient). Clinician interviews and retrospective review of medical records were undertaken to assess for occurrence of side effects, which were graded according to the recommendations of published guidelines for standardisation of IMT trials. Data regarding treatment interruption and increase in asthma rescue medication use was also collected. Results: No systemic side effects were reported in any of the nine patients. No patients required treatment interruption or modification as a consequence of any adverse reactions to SLIT. Asthma rescue medication use was not increased in any of the patients. Conclusion: In this highly selected group of nine patients with FEV1 < 70% predicted, SLIT has been safely administered without any systemic side effects or exacerbations of asthma as assessed by rescue medication use. Further prospective studies are warranted to investigate the safety of SLIT in the population with FEV1 < 70% predicted.

A second treatment course leads to further reduction of the combined symptom and medication score.
Efficacy and safety of grass monomeric allergoid sublingual immunotherapy: A randomised study comparing two different treatment regimens versus drug therapy alone; Background: Monomeric allergoid sublingual immunotherapy (allergoid SLIT) proved to be well tolerated, safe and effective in patients with respiratory allergy. A drawback is that the achievement of a clinical benefit using a standard regimen requires a long time before efficacy may be appreciated. Aim of this study was to investigate whether different regimens of allergoid SLIT (i.e. perennial versus preseasonal) may affect the clinical outcome. Methods: Thirty-three adult patients (mean age 29 ± 10.1 years, 13 F) with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis with/without mild intermittent asthma were enrolled into the study and randomised to receive either allergoid SLIT with a perennial regimen (group 1: 10 patients, 1000 AU/week for 2 years, for a total amount of 100 000 UA) or allergoid SLIT with a pre-seasonal regimen (group 2: 11 patients, 5000 AU/week for 10 weeks/year for 2 years, for a total amount of 104 000 UA) or drug therapy alone (group 3: 11 patients). At baseline and at the end of the second pollen season a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) was performed to assess the patients' well-being. Symptom score (sneezing, rhinorrea, nasal congestion, ocular symptoms, cough, asthma symptoms) and drug consumption (antihistamines, broncodilators, nasal, bronchial and oral corticosteroids) were also evaluated with monthly diary cards. Adverse reactions (ARs) were recorded. Results: One patient of group 1 dropped-out after the randomisation because of two mild ARs (paresthesia at the lips and sorethroat with burning). The statistical analysis was thus performed on 32 patients. There was a significant VAS improvement in both group 1 and 2 after one and 2 years of treatment compared to the baseline and group 3 values (P < 0.05). Furthermore, group 1 and 2 patients had less symptoms in comparison to group 3 at the second year, being the difference statistically significant (P < 0.05). In addition there was a significant reduction of drug consumption in group 1 and 2 versus group 3 at the second year (P < 0.05). No severe AR has been observed. Conclusion: Both perennial and pre-seasonal grass allergoid SLIT showed to be effective, safe and well tolerated.

Lack of association between clinical efficacy and cellular immune responses in the blood during grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy; Background: The efficacy of a 300-IR 5-grass-pollen SLIT tablet on rhinoconjonctivitis symptoms was confirmed in a double blind, placebo controlled study conducted in an allergen challenge chamber (ACC). We took advantage of this study to inquire whether changes in basophil activation and T cell responses can be used as biomarkers predicting efficacy. Methods: Changes in immunological markers were investigated in 82 patients with grass pollen-related allergic rhinoconjunctivitis who received active or placebo tablets sublingually once a day for four months. An allergen challenge with grass pollen was performed in the Vienna Challenge Chamber (VCC) at baseline, after 1 week, and after 1, 2 and 4 months of treatment. Blood samples were collected before treatment and after 2 and 4 treatment months for assessment of basophil activation (based on CD203c expression) and T cell responses (looking at proliferation, pheno-type, cytokine production and gene expression). Results: SLIT with a 5-grass-pollen tablet led to significant improvement (versus placebo) of 29.8% for the mean average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) at end point. Clinical responders were defined as the 25% of patients with the highest relative improvement in symptom score from baseline, corresponding to at least a 48.9% decrease of ARTSS after treatment. No changes in basophil activation and T-cell proliferation were noticed for active and placebo groups in response to either the extract, Dac g 1 or Dac g 5 allergens, during treatment. Higher expression of Treg markers (eg Foxp 3) and lower expression of molecules associated with a Th1/Th2 profile were observed during treatment for both active and placebo groups. PMBCs from patients exposed to active treatment (versus placebo) displayed a lower production of TNF-alpha and a higher expression of IFN-gamma, with no differences between responders and non responders. All patients with a high symptom score before treatment responded to SLIT. However, neither basophil activation nor levels of T cell proliferation prior to treatment were predictive of efficacy. Conclusion: Basophil activation and T cell responses measured in the blood are not predictive of clinical responses induced by SLIT. Our results do not preclude that changes in cellular responses monitored in target respiratory mucosae can account for SLIT efficacy.
Heterogeneity of antibody responses among clinical responders following grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy; Background: Biomarkers of clinical efficacy are of major interest to monitor patients under specific sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT). To identify such surrogates, we investigated seric and mucosal antibody responses in the context of a randomised, double-blind placebo-controlled study conducted in an allergen challenge chamber. Methods: Changes in titres and affinity of allergen-specific IgE, IgG1-4, IgM and IgA were monitored in serum and nasal secretions in a cohort of 82 grass pollen allergic patients receiving once daily a sublingual 300IR grass pollen tablet or a placebo for 4 months. Average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) was evaluated before and after 1 week, 1, 2 and 4 months of treatment, during allergen challenges in a pollen chamber. Results: A significant clinical response was observed in the group receiving the active treatment. The latter was documented in patients exhibiting distinct patterns of IgE sensitization (i.e. narrow, intermediate, broad) against Phl p 1 to 12 allergens. No neosensitization to grass pollen allergens was observed in the course of SLIT. Responders were defined as the 25% of patients with the highest relative improvement in symptom score from baseline, corresponding to at least a 48.9% decrease of ARTSS after treatment. Comparing antibody responses from patients belonging to each of the four following groups: Placebo responders/Placebo non responders/Active responders/Active non responders, we could establish that (i) Placebo responders exhibit clear grass pollen-specific antibody responses in nasal mucosa and (ii) Active responders are heterogeneous, encompassing both 'immunoreactive' patients with strong grass pollen-specific IgG, IgE and IgG4 responses (possibly blocking antibodies) induced during SLIT, as well as 'non immunoreactive' responders with no detectable immune responses distinguishing them from patients receiving placebo. Importantly, patients with high symptoms scores at inclusion were all improved under SLIT, although specific IgE levels prior to treatment were not predictive. Conclusion: SLIT with a grass pollen extract is similarly efficacious in patients exhibiting sensitization to single or multiple grass pollen allergens. Responders include both patients with strong seric allergen-specific antibody responses or lacking such responses. The latter observation suggests that additional immune mechanisms distinct from blocking antibodies are involved in SLIT efficacy.

There were benefits in having a group of 20 children all starting treatment at the same time and from the same area of the country. The pollen counts were obtained to compare symptom scoring with them and demonstrated that those patients with previously unmanaged SAR had much better control. Patients also utilised their questionnaires to comment on other family members' symptoms being present when theirs were not, contrary to their normal seasonal history. Persistence of specific grass pollen immunotherapies are similar to those observed in other long-term treatment regimens; Background: Specific immunotherapy (SIT) is a valid treatment option for moderateto-severe seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis (SAR) caused by grass pollen. However, there are few data on persistence with long-term SIT regimens. Methods: Individual prescriptions/refill as a proxy for persistence (i.e. defined as the length of time during which the patient continues to be engaged with the prescribed dosing regimen) for three different SIT modalities (subcutaneous immunotherapy immunotherapy (SCIT) with natural allergens, SCIT with modified allergens (allergoids) and sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) with natural pollen extract solutions) were retrospectively tracked over 3 years (2005, 2006 and 2007) in a representative database of patients in Germany (INSIGHT Health). We determined whether SIT-naive patients receiving their first immunotherapy prescription in 2005 had renewed it for the same product group in 2006 and again in 2007. Results: A total of 1410 patients started SIT in 2005 with 112, 695 and 602 for natural extract SLIT, natural extract SCIT and allergoid SCIT, respectively). The distribution of the patients across the three groups reflects the documented market shares for these three SIT modalities in Germany. In 2006, the prescription renewal rates were 71%, 55% and 59%, respectively. In 2007, the rates (relative to 2005) were 51%, 34% and 39%. There were no significant differences between natural extract SCIT and allergoid SCIT (P = 0.1665 in 2006 and P = 0.0605 in 2007, in a chi-squared test) in terms of renewal. Prescription renewal rates for natural extract SLIT were significantly higher than those for natural extract SCIT (P = 0.0015 for 2006 and P = 0.0003 for 2007) and allergoid SCIT (P = 0.0152 for 2006 and P = 0.0111 for 2007). These findings confirm the issue of non-persistence with therapy in other chronic diseases in which non persistence at 6 months after start of therapy is as high as 50%. Conclusion: In a representative, German prescription database, all grass pollen SCIT and SLIT modalities displayed similar long-term prescription renewal rates to those observed in other chronic therapeutic regimens (diabetes, cardiovascular disease and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, for example). Furthermore, our prescription renewal rate data counter the preconceived notion that SCIT (with injection in a medical environment) necessarily results in better overall persistence than SLIT (usually administered at home).

The clinical development of specific immunotherapies: Specific methodological issues and clinical interpretation of results; Background: Historically, the safety and efficacy of specific immunotherapy (SIT) has been demonstrated in (mainly small-scale) studies and confirmed in meta-analyses. However, the inherent sources of heterogeneity (patient selection outside the pollen season, pollen count variations, long evaluation periods) observed in recent, large-scale studies of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) tablets mean that highly susceptible patients may not exhibit uniformly a sufficient level of symptoms during the study period to assess the efficacy of SIT. Methods: We performed randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational clinical trials of a 300IR pre- and co-seasonally administered 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet in adults and children with allergic rhinitis. The primary efficacy criterion was the mean average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) over the pollen season, during which daily grass pollen counts were measured locally. To evaluate the potential relationship between disease severity and the treatment effect, investigating centres were divided in tiertiles according to their mean placebo group ARTSS. Results: Pre-seasonal inclusion of patients on the basis of retrospectively severe symptoms in the previous pollen season did not produce such a severely affected population in the study season. The apparent treatment effect of SLIT tablet was partially masked by the highly variable severity of symptoms during the whole pollen season (mean ARTSS in the adult placebo group: 4.93 ± 3.229). For the adult trial, the mean active versus placebo ARTSSs and the relative difference versus placebo (%) were 15%, 26% and 37% for the low, moderate- and high-disease severity tiertiles, respectively. In the paediatric trial, these values were 10%, 33% and 34%, respectively. Linear regression of individual daily RTSS scores and pollen counts in active and placebo groups also showed that the more severe the disease, the greater the treatment effect of SLIT tablet. Conclusion: Inherent sources of heterogeneity must be taken into account when interpreting the results of natural-exposure immunotherapy trials but none obscured the statistically significant treatment effect of SLIT. In a subgroup analysis, SLIT tablets' beneficial effect increased with disease severity.

▼Grazax for hay fever - What's new?; In 2008, we reviewed Grazax, a sublingual tablet containing standardised allergen extract of grass pollen.1 At the time, this product was licensed for the treatment of adults with proven grass-pollen-induced rhinitis and conjunctivitis (hay fever). However, we were not convinced that the effect on rhinoconjunctivitis symptom scores in published trials was clinically relevant. Also, given that no published studies had compared Grazax with symptomatic therapies or subcutaneous immunotherapy for hay fever, it was expensive and its long-term efficacy and safety were not known, we could not recommend its use.1 Since our review, the terms of the marketing authorisation for Grazax have been changed, such that it is now described in the summary of product characteristics (SPC) as a "disease-modifying treatment", and the drug is now also licensed for use in children aged 5 years and above.2 Here we assess the latest evidence for Grazax and reconsider the drug's place in the management of patients with hay fever.

Clinical parameters to evaluate the efficacy of allergen-specific immunotherapy in allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Calculation of "well days" as an adjunct concept; Efficacy monitoring of immunotherapy (IT) is performed to adjust the therapy according to the patients reactions, to collect data for scientific studies and to evaluate the efficacy of IT. A decrease of allergy symptoms and of drug use are the main efficacy parameters obtained by using the symptom-medication-score (SMS). For this, allergy diaries, skin tests and nasal provocation testing are most suitable. During the period of documentation pollen exposition should be monitored with Burkhard traps. In cytologic measures specific cell activation markers and specific lymphokine-profiles can be evaluated. For the reason of their expense, those methods are restricted to scientific investigations and only rarely for routine diagnostics. Numerous clinical trials have investigated the efficacy and safety of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) using symptom- and medication-scores. The results suggest that high allergen doses are necessary to achieve adequate efficacy. An alternative approach to assess the outcome of allergen-specific immunotherapy was investigated by a new high-dose sublingual 6-grass pollen preparation. This sublingual immunotherapy significantly improved the symptom-medication-score (SMS) in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial by counting "well days" (days without intake of any rescue medication and a reduction of the symptom-score) during the grass pollen season. This post-hoc analysis showed that SLIT for 1.5 years resulted in a significantly higher number of "well days" than with placebo. These results reflect the high improvement in symptom-medication-score. "Well days" can therefore be regarded as a further variable to measure efficacy of allergen-specific immunotherapy. © 2010 Dustri-Verlag Dr. Karl Feistle.

Treatment with the SQ-standardised grass allergy immunotherapy tablet in children above and below the age of 10 - Efficacy, safety and immunological response; Purpose: Treatment with the SQ-standardised grass allergen immunotherapy tablet (AIT), GRAZAX® (Phleum pratense 75,000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU, ALK, Denmark), is efficacious and well-tolerated in grass allergic patients. Results: Analysis of the difference between active and placebo for each age group showed a slightly higher relative difference in symptom score for the younger children compared with the older, 26% versus 19%. In the AIT group the percentage of adverse events assessed as treatment-related was nominally lower for the younger group than for the older, 32% versus 40%. Rationale for five-grass pollen vaccine; Grass pollen. allergic patients are naturally exposed and sensitized to multiple pollens from various Pooideae species. The question arises as to whether such patients should be desensitized with extracts based on a single pollen or a pollen mixture. Neither conventional diagnosis based on IgE reactivity nor pollen counts enable the identification of which grass species are involved in patient sensitization. Significant cross-immunogenicity is observed between allergens from Pooideae pollens due to their conserved amino acid sequences (e.g. > 90% for group 1, 55-80% for group 5, 30-60% for other allergens, including minor allergens). Nevertheless, pollen allergens also contain species-specific T or B cell epitopes, and there is evidence that at least 50% of allergic patients are sensitized to such distinct epitopes. In addition, substantial quantitative differences exist in the allergen (e.g. group 1, 2/3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 13) content of pollens obtained from distinct grass species. In this context, we recommend a vaccine consisting of a combination of pollens from five common and well characterized Pooideae including Anthoxanthum odoratum, Dactylis glomerata, Lolium perenne, Phleum pratense and Poa pratensis for desensitization purposes. The SQ-standardized grass allergy immunotherapy tabletis well tolerated over 3 years of treatment; Introduction: Traditionally, allergen-specific immunotherapy has been administered via subcutaneous injections or sublingual drops. Recently, a new formulation administered sublingually, allergy immunotherapy tablets (AIT), has emerged. Many large double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials have demonstrated AIT to be well tolerated and efficacious in reducing rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms and the use of rescue medications. We investigated the nature, severity and duration of the most common adverse events (AEs) associated with treatment with an SQ-standardized grass AIT (Phleum pratense, 75,000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU, ALK, Denmark) during a trial conducted over a 3 year period. Methods: Subjects with grass-allergy (n=634) were enrolled in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational trial, of which 351 continued in a 2-year extension. Approval was obtained from the local IRBs and written informed consent obtained from all subjects. Subjects were randomized 1:1 to grass AIT or placebo. All AEs were collected and rated as mild, moderate or severe. AEs were assessed as treatment-emergent if the start date was on or after the date of the first tablet intake. Reactions occurring for a limited period of time each day on consecutive days were reported as one event. Results: The most frequent AEs after grass AIT were oral pruritus (164 subjects, 191 events), mouth edema (65 subjects, 70 events), ear pruritus (41 subjects, 42 events) and throat irritation (34 subjects, 37 events). The majority of these AEs were mild (84%) or moderate (13%) and transient of nature. There was a sharp decrease in the percentage of subjects reporting these AEs within the first weeks ofthe trial (figure). Conclusions: The most frequent AEs after grass AIT were local reactions affecting the mucosal membranes in mouth, ear and throat. The majority of AEs were mild and generally subsided shortly after treatment initiation, indicating development of tolerance. A small proportion of the subjects experienced local AEs daily upon tablet administration. However, the rate of withdrawals due to local AEs was low, indicating that grass AIT was well tolerated and these side effects were acceptable to most patients. (Figure Presented).

Efficacy of grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy for three consecutive seasons and after cessation of treatment: The ECRIT study; Background: Data supporting a carry-over effect with sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) are scarce. Methods: Patients (7.9-64.7 years) with grass pollen allergy received ultra-rush titration with increasing doses (30, 90, 150 and 300 IR) of a 5-grass pollen mixture every 20 min at the start of the pollen seasons, followed by 300 IR daily until the end of the pollen seasons. A baseline season (no SLIT) was followed by three consecutive treatment seasons and one follow-up season. Symptoms, medication and adverse events were documented and specific immunoglobulin (Ig)E and IgG4 measured. Results: Data were analysed for 183 of the 213 randomized patients. Mean treatment duration varied between seasons (81.8-92.7 days). Combined scores (symptoms and medication) improved progressively across treatment seasons (up to 44.7% improvement for SLIT compared with baseline) and fluctuated between -11.3% and -14.8% for placebo (P < 0.05). Similar changes were observed for symptom scores, with a successive decrease of 39.7% (SLIT) and fluctuations between +13.6% and -1.51% for placebo (P < 0.05). Combined score (P = 0.0508) and symptom score improvements (P = 0.0144) with SLIT continued during follow up. Increases in specific IgG4 observed in the first season were sustained for SLIT vs placebo throughout treatment (P = 0.0001). Titration and daily SLIT were well tolerated. No serious systemic or anaphylactic reactions were reported. Conclusions: Seasonal SLIT with ultra-rush titration is well tolerated and effective from the first treatment season onwards. Slowing progression along the allergic disease continuum: Quo vadit immunotherapy?; There is emerging evidence that rhinitis frequently precedes the onset of asthmatic symptoms. The frequent association of rhinitis and asthma has led to the concept that these conditions are likely manifestations of the same disease. This hypothesis has important implications for both the diagnosis and the management of these common conditions. Unfortunately, there is little known regarding the risk factors responsible for the progression of rhinitis to asthma. The current treatment options can control symptoms but do not prevent or cure the disease. However, there is recent data supporting the notion that it is possible to prevent new asthma cases by modifying the immune response and clinical outcome with allergen immunotherapy. This review article evaluates the impact of rhinitis on the development of asthma, examines putative predictors for the progression of rhinitis to asthma, and reviews recent, promising literature suggesting that early treatment of allergic individuals with immunotherapy may aid in asthma prevention. © 2009 Mary Ann Liebert, Inc.

Recombinant allergens for following antibody-responses during immunotherapywith a grass pollen vaccine and after five years of discontinuation; Objectives: Follow-up of antibody responses in serum samples from grass pollen allergic patients having received one course of injection immunotherapy (SIT) with an aluminium hydroxide-adsorbed grass pollen extract (n=12) or only anti-inflammatory treatment (n=7). Serum samples were taken before treatment, after five months of treatment and after five years. Methods: Specific IgE, IgG1-IgG4, IgM, IgA and light chain responses were monitored using purified recombinant timothy grass (i.e., Phl p 1, Phl p 2, Phl p 5, Phl p 6, Phl p 7, Phl p 12, Phl p 13)- and birch pollen (Bet v 1) allergens. Results: After five months of SIT but not after inflammatory treatment we found increases of IgG1 > IgG4 > IgG2 antibody responses in particular for the major grass pollen allergens Phl p 1, Phl p 5, Phl p 6 and Phl p 2 but no relevant increases against the other tested allergens (Phl p 7, Phl p 12, Phl p 13, Bet v 1). Thus only SIT but not anti-inflammatory treatment has disease-modifying effects.

Here, we review literature from the past 5 years to determine the differences between standard extract SCIT and more recent formulations. Methods: Research articles on PubMed published during the last 5 years which reported clinical endpoints from SCIT regimens for SAR were selected and reviewed. SCIT formulations included allergen extracts, recombinant allergens, allergoids and adjuvanted allergoids. Results: Reduction in symptoms, medication usage or a combination of the two were commonly used as clinical outcome measures. SCIT was typically found to reduce symptoms or combined symptom/medication scores by ∼30% more than placebo and to be effective in over 80% of patients after one season of therapy. All regimens were well tolerated, and serious adverse reactions were generally rare. Fewer systemic and serious adverse reactions occurred following allergoid-based therapy compared with allergen-based preparations. The uSCIT (adjuvanted allergoid) formulation had the lowest injection burden and was one of two formulations which did not require ongoing maintenance therapy during the pollen season after the induction period. Conclusions: Developing technologies in SCIT have made this mode of therapy a more convenient and realistic option for SAR patients. The clinical efficacy of SCIT has been known for some time. However, practical restraints on its administration have made conventional SCIT relatively inconvenient. uSCIT appears to offer all of the clinical benefits of conventional SCIT but without many of the practical drawbacks, and can be given safely to appropriately-selected patients.

Methods: Patient selection: Seventy-two male and female patients aged 20-63 years with hay fever due to grass pollen sensitization were enrolled based on a mild to moderate response upon 4000 Dactylis glomerata pollen grains/m3 within 2 h in the ECC. Main exclusion criteria: Clinically significant sensitization against tree pollen, weed pollen and perennial allergens, persistent asthma (GINA ≥II). Treatment: Immunotherapy was performed using 1000 DPP/ml depigmented and polymerized allergenic extract of grass pollen. Primary outcome was the change from baseline in the median 'Total Nasal Symptom Score' (TNSS) during the allergen challenge which consists of the 4 symptoms nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, nasal itching, sneezing each scored on a 100 mm visual analogue scale (VAS) ranging from 'none' to 'severe'. Results: Analysis was based on the PP set (N = 69) using a nonparametric test (Median test). Median baseline TNSS for the active group was 152 and for the placebo group 159. Defining responders with an improvement of 30% in TNSS a statistical significant difference between treatment groups could be observed: 23/35 (66%) active and 13/34 (38%) placebo patients responded (P < 0.03). Eleven patients of the Depiquick Grass Mix and 10 of the placebo group developed mild systemic reactions s.a. rhinitis, conjunctivitis, headache, hoarseness and pruritus. Conclusions: Short-term rush immunotherapy with Depiquick Grass Mix was effective and safe as determined by means of ECC evaluation.

Does allergen specific immunotherapy influence clinical chemistry and haematology laboratory parameters in adults?; Background: A standard clinical variable in clinical trials with products for allergen specific immunotherapy (SIT) is the measurement of allergen specific antibody response. In addition, the upcoming European Medicines Agency (EMEA) guideline on the clinical development of products for SIT requested the performance of more general safety laboratory including haematology and blood chemistry tests. We checked laboratory variables of two clinical trials with two different routes of application of grass and birch pollen extract to address the question whether SIT has an impact on routine laboratory parameters. Methods: Thirteen haematological laboratory parameters and eight clinical chemistry parameters were evaluated from two double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised, multi-centre, phase III clinical trials with 373 patients in total suffering from allergic rhinoconjunctivitis with or without asthma. The status at baseline was compared with the values obtained at the end of the double blind study phase. A sum of 162 patients were treated with a high-dose sublingual grass pollen preparation or placebo for 14 months. The other 211 patients were treated with a subcutaneous hypoallergenic birch pollen allergoid or placebo for 2 years. Gamma GT was measured only in the study with the subcutaneous hypoallergenic birch pollen preparation. Median values of each parameter from baseline and after treatment were compared. Differences in the median values of more than 10% were discussed. Results: SIT with a high-dose sublingual grass pollen preparation or a subcutaneous hypoallergenic birch pollen allergoid did not show an influence on any of the 21 laboratory parameters analysed here from two studies. Conclusion: The evaluation of these parameters during the screening-process of clinical trials is essential in view of potential contraindications. The need for repeated measurement of these parameters after SIT routinely in each clinical trial during the development process may be subject of consideration, at least for preparation from natural sources as evaluated here.
Grass allergen tablet immunotherapy in children induces IgG4 antibody and 4IgE-blocking responses similar to those seen in adults; Background: Serum antibody responses were investigated after ALK grass allergen tablet immunotherapy (AIT), Grazax (Phleum pratense 75 000 SQ-T/2800 BAU, ALK-Abelló) in children and results compared to those obtained after the same treatment in adults. Methods: In randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multi-centre trials in children (5-16 year) and adults (18-65 year), AIT was initiated prior to the grass pollen season, and once-daily treatment was continued until the end of the season. All participants had a clinical history of moderate to severe grass allergy. The levels of Phleum pratense specific IgG4 and IgE-blocking factor (i.e. serum components competing with IgE for allergen binding) were assessed in serum samples before, during and after the grass pollen season. Results: In children, specific IgG4 was significantly increased from the initial level at all assessments after treatment initiation in the active group (P < 0.001). The increase after 7.3 months of treatment was 32 U/l. In adults, 8 months of treatment led to an increase in the active group of 45.7 U/l from the initial level (P < 0.001). The IgE-blocking factor increased in the active AIT groups in both children and adults (significantly different treatment effect in the active groups compared to the placebo groups, P < 0.001 in both trials). In children the difference from the initial level in IgE-blocking factor in the active group was 0.25 after 7.3 months, while in adults the difference was 0.15 after 8 months. The adult placebo group showed no significant change while the paediatric placebo group showed a slight increase in IgE-blocking factor during the grass pollen season. The clinical treatment effect in children by means of the rhinoconjunctivitis symptom score and the percentage of well days was also similar to that observed in adults when looking at comparable pollen exposure periods. Conclusion: These data confirm comparable elevations in serum IgG4 antibodies and IgE-blocking activity in children compared with adults following successful treatment with ALK grass AIT. In addition, the higher seasonal elevations in IgE-blocking activity in placebo-treated children compared with adults, suggest that children may establish a more tolerogenic rather than allergic immune response during the grass pollen season. This observation suggests that the use of AIT in childhood may ameliorate the ongoing natural course of the disease more efficiently than AIT during adulthood.

The effect of the matched pairs method on the measurement of treatment effect in a trial of ultra short course specific immunotherapy; Background: A common problem during the assessment of specific immunotherapy (SIT) in patients with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis is incomplete data from patient diaries during the pollen season. Such data gaps may be filled using the matched pairs method, but this process has the potential to distort the data and invite misleading conclusions. Here we compare whole-population, matched-pair data from a large Phase III trial with the subgroup of patients for whom complete data were available to assess the effect of the matched pairs method. Methods: In a large, randomised, Phase III trial, 1028 patients with moderate-to-severe allergic rhinoconjunctivitis to grass pollen received ultra short course specific immunotherapy (uSCIT) or placebo. Efficacy was measured using a combined symptom and medication score (CSMS) from patient diary data collected during the four peak weeks of pollen exposure. We compared data for the whole population, which utilised a matched pairs method to fill data gaps, with data from the subset of subjects for whom complete data were available. Results: There were 343 subjects for whom 28 diary entries were available during the four peak weeks of the pollen season (177 uSCIT, 166 placebo). In both the whole population and the complete data subgroup, uSCIT was found to be significantly more effective than placebo, with improvements in the CSMS of 13.4% (P = 0.0038) and 26.9% (P = 0.0031) for the whole population and complete data groups, respectively. There was a similar pattern for symptom scores alone (eyes and nose), with improvements for uSCIT compared with placebo of 10.9% (P = 0.0132) and 24.7% (P = 0.0181) for the whole population and complete data groups, respectively. Conclusion: The disparity in the primary endpoint between the whole population and the subgroup with complete data was considerable. Although a significant benefit for uSCIT compared with placebo was detected in each set of data, the size of the effect was approximately doubled when complete data were used to compare the treatment groups. It is therefore apparent that using the matched pairs method to compensate for incomplete data may not improve the precision of the estimate of treatment effect for the whole population, in this case yielding a 50% underestimate of treatment efficacy in approximately one third of subjects. This phenomenon represents a significant challenge in the assessment of SIT formulations for allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.
Efficacy of sublingual immunotherapy with a high-dose 6-grass pollen preparation progressively increases in the third treatment year; Background: Efficacy of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) depends on a sufficiently high maintenance dose as recently confirmed by the ARIA workshop report (2008 update). Often SLIT trials last for at most 2 years, and only few data are available about the effect of further treatment years. Progressive efficacy of a high-dose Single Dose grass pollen preparation has been shown in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial for the first two treatment years. The preparation was standardized to the content of 40 μg grasses group 5 allergens in the maintenance dose. Aim of this study was to investigate the effect of a third treatment year. Methods: After a baseline period in 2003 grass pollen-allergic patients (rhinoconjunctivitis with or without asthma) received treatment with AllerSlit forte or placebo for two consecutive years (2004 and 2005). Data from 39 of the former 49 actively treated patients in the Main Data Set (MDS) were available in the third, open treatment year (2006). Symptom and medication scores, and the number of 'well days' (days with a symptom score ≤4 and without use of any rescue medication) were evaluated. Results: Symptom and medication scores were further improved during the third treatment year in comparison to the year before. The percentage of patients who did not need any rescue medication during the 42-day observation period in the grass pollen season continuously increased during the study: 0% at baseline, 19% at the end of the double-blind phase in 2005 to 31% in the third treatment year. Additionally, the median number of 'well days' increased during the 3 years: from 6/42 days at baseline pollen season, and 19.5/42 days after two treatment years in 2005 to 35/42 'well days' after 3 years of SLIT. The high-dose preparation was well tolerated with mainly mild adverse reactions. No serious drugrelated adverse events occurred. Conclusion: The third year of SLIT with the high-dose grass pollen preparation caused an additional benefit for the patients. Allergic symptoms and the intake of rescue medication were further reduced during the grass pollen season. The high number of 'well days' affirms the progressive efficacy.

Relation between grass pollen exposure and efficacy for a grass allergen immunotherapy tablet; Background: Pollen levels display extreme day-to-day variation. Hence, post hoc analyses exploring the effect of grass pollen exposure on efficacy measures and observed differences between treatment groups were performed for a phase III trial investigating the efficacy and safety in children of the once-daily ALK grass allergen immunotherapy tablet (AIT), Grazax (Phleum pratense, 75,000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU). Methods: A total of 253 children aged 5-16 years with grass allergy were randomised 1 : 1 to receive either active treatment or placebo prior to and throughout the grass pollen season 2007. Symptomatic medications were provided as rescue medication to both groups in a step-wise fashion. Statistical analyses of efficacy parameters were performed with two different definitions of the pollen season, using 10 or 30 grains/m3 as threshold. In addition, the effect of pollen exposure was explored by investigating the efficacy for days with low, medium and high pollen counts and by modelling the dependence of the efficacy scores on the pollen count for each treatment group. Results: Statistically significant differences between active and placebo demonstrated effect of the ALK grass AIT throughout the entire grass pollen season for both pollen season definitions. The definition of the pollen season influenced the efficacy outcome. Using 10 grains/m3, the relative differences between active and placebo were 22% for both the mean symptom score and for well days. These differences increased upon replacing the threshold with 30 grains/m3, to 28% for the symptom score and 44% for well days. On days with high pollen counts (>50 grains/m3), symptoms increased compared to days with low pollen counts (≤10 grains/m3), from a daily average of 2.1 to 3.8 for the placebo group and from 1.7 to 2.7 for the active group. Simultaneously the average medication score increased from 0.8 to 2.4 for the placebo group but only from 0.4 to 0.9 for the active group. Modelling of the efficacy scores showed a substantial increase in the difference between active and placebo upon increasing pollen load. Conclusion: This was the first phase III trial investigating the ALK grass AIT in children. A clear statistically significant difference between active and placebo was seen throughout the entire grass pollen season, in favour of active treatment. On days with high pollen counts the clinical benefit of the ALK grass AIT was markedly increased, both for symptoms and for the use of symptomatic medication.
Treatment with a grass allergen immunotherapy tablet in children above and below the age of 10 - efficacy, safety and immunological response; Background: Treatment with the ALK grass allergen immunotherapy tablet (AIT), Grazax (Phleum pratense, 75,000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU), is efficacious and well-tolerated in adult grass-allergic patients. Younger children are often perceived as good candidates for immunotherapy, and post hoc analyses to explore possible differences between younger and older children were performed for an ALK grass AIT paediatric phase III trial. Methods: A total of 253 children aged 5-16 years with grass allergy were randomised 1 : 1 to receive either active treatment or placebo prior to and throughout the grass pollen season 2007. Symptomatic medications were provided as rescue medication to both groups. The population was divided into two age groups comprising 140 children aged 5-10 years and 113 children aged 11-16 years. The effect of age on efficacy was also analysed by including age as a covariate in the symptom score analysis. Results: Including age as a covariate in the symptom score analysis indicated age to have no influence on the efficacy, as demonstrated by a P-value of 0.6 for the interaction between age and treatment. Analysis of the difference between active and placebo for each age group showed a slightly higher relative difference in symptom score for the younger children compared with the older, 26% versus 19%. The difference between active and placebo was statistically significant for the 5-10 year old (P = 0.047) although the trial was powered for analysis of the population as a whole. In the active group the percentage of adverse events (AEs) assessed as treatment-related was nominally lower for the younger group than for the older children, 32% versus 40%. The percentages of AEs assessed as moderate or severe in the active group were similar for the two age groups. For both active and placebo, the overall number of AEs was nominally higher in the younger group than in the older group. The immunological response (IgE, IgG4 and IgE-blocking factor) was similar for the two age groups. There was a tendency for the younger group towards an increased response in IgE-blocking factor with onset of the grass pollen season, evident in both the actively treated and the placebo group. Conclusion: This was the first phase III trial investigating the ALK grass AIT in children. Once-daily administration was found to be clinically efficacious and welltolerated. The effect was comparable for children below and above the age of 10, as was the safety pattern and the immunological response.

In-season initiation of treatment with SQ standardised grass allergy immunotherapy tablet induces an immunomodulatory response and seems to be well tolerated; Background: Clinical efficacy and a favourable safety profile of the SQ standardised grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT, Grazax®, Phleum pratense 75,000 SQ-T, ALK-Abelló) have been demonstrated in several trials. The current recommendation is to start treatment 4 months prior to the grass pollen season and to continue treatment for 3 consecutive years. A large proportion of allergy patients have their first visit to the physician during the pollen season, i.e. when they experience their symptoms. Currently, these subjects are offered symptomatic therapy and the opportunity to start immunotherapy after the pollen season. For these patients, it would be of interest to be able to start treatment in the season. Therefore, in the present trial the pharmacodynamic effect and tolerability of in-season initiation of AIT treatment were evaluated. Methods: The trial was a parallel-group, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial conducted in 28 centres in Germany and Austria. A total of 276 subjects with grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis with or without asthma were randomised 4 : 1 to receive either active (N = 219) or placebo (N = 57) once daily, starting during the grass pollen season and continuing at least 8 weeks (+ 1-2 weeks). Pharmacodynamic endpoints included the change from baseline of IgE-blocking factor, IgE, and IgG4. Tolerability assessment was based on adverse events. Results: An immunomodulatory effect of in-season treatment was demonstrated with statistically significant higher inductions of IgE-blocking factor (P < 0.0001), IgE (P < 0.0001) and IgG4 (P <.0001) in the active group as compared with placebo. Overall, in-season treatment was well tolerated and comparable to what has been observed in other clinical trials in which treatment was initiated outside the pollen season. Most of the reported adverse events were mild or moderate in severity. The majority of events related to treatment were local reactions, mainly oral pruritus. Four serious adverse events, all considered unlikely related to treatment, were reported during the trial. No safety concerns were observed regarding FEV1, vital sign or physical examinations. Conclusion: In-season initiation of treatment with the grass AIT induces an immunomodulatory response in subjects with grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis. Furthermore, in-season initiation was found to be well tolerated, however a suitable powered trial would be required to confirm the safety profile.

An economic evaluation of grazax for the treatment of grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis in children; OBJECTIVES: To determine the cost-effectiveness of the grass allergen immunotherapy tablet (AIT), Grazax (ALK-Abelló A/S) for the treatment of grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis in children either with or without co-existing asthma. The analysis compares treatment using Grazax in combination with symptomatic medications, to using symptomatic medications alone in terms of costs and health outcomes. METHODS: The model uses a decision tree structure to evaluate two grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis treatments for a cohort of 1000 hypothetical children. The analysis is performed from the perspective of the payer, including only direct costs in the base case. Treatment is modelled in terms of the management of symptoms, reduction in resource use and averting the development of allergic asthma. The evaluation is UK-based and models both short- and long-term effects. Several data inputs, such as resource use and probabilities, are drawn from the paediatric GT-12 clinical trial and the Preventive Allergy Treatment (PAT) study. Cost data are sourced from established published sources and utility values are derived using GT-12 trial data and a published study. RESULTS: Treatment with Grazax in combination with symptomatic medications compared to treatment with symptomatic medications alone generates a (discounted) incremental cost per QALY gained of 10,007GBP ($14,578, ε11,034), for the base case time horizon of nine years. The QALY gains are a result of increased quality of life related to effective symptom management. The sensitivity analysis carried out around key parameters (e.g. unit costs, medication costs, probabilities, utilities) shows that the results estimated by the model remain robust. CONCLUSIONS: Grazax has been shown to improve patient outcomes, at an increased cost. The resulting incremental cost per QALY falls below commonly accepted willingness to pay thresholds. Therefore, Grazax is a cost-effective option for the treatment of grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis in the UK paediatric population.

Implementation of pre-seasonal sublingual immunotherapy with a five-grass pollen tablet during optimal dosage assessment; Background: The optimal dose (300IR) of a five-grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy tablet in terms of efficacy was previously demonstrated from the first pollen season. Objective: Here, we aim to confirm whether this dose remained optimal during the peak of the pollen season by assessing the efficacy and quality of life data. Methods: A total of 628 subjects with grass pollen rhinoconjunctivitis were randomized in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-centre, pan-European trial. Subjects received once-daily tablets (Stallergenes, Antony, France) of 100IR, 300IR, 500IR or placebo, starting 4 months before and throughout the 2005 grass pollen season. The pollen season was defined as the first day of 3 consecutive days with a grass pollen count above 30 grains/m3 of air, recorded using Hirst-type volumetric pollen traps, to the last day before 3 consecutive days with a pollen count below 30 grains/m3. Results: The grass pollen season lasted an average of 30 days, with a peak of 12 days. The mean treatment duration before the grass pollen season was similar in the four treatment groups (121.4±31.1 to 128.6±15.4 days in the safety population). Both the 300IR and 500IR groups had highly significant improvements in Rhinoconjunctivitis Total Symptom Score (RTSS) vs. placebo at the peak pollen season (P=0.0005 and 0.0014, respectively), which agreed with improvements in RTSS in the primary evaluations. The average RTSS scores were slightly elevated during the peak pollen season in all treatment groups. The overall Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire score confirmed the optimal dosage 300IR at peak (P<0.0001) and at the end (P≤0.0031) of the pollen season. All doses were well tolerated. Conclusion: At the peak pollen season, the efficacy and quality of life data for both 300IR and 500IR groups was significantly improved vs. the placebo group. These results confirm the conclusions of the primary evaluations and validate the use of 300IR tablets for clinical practice. © 2008 Stallergenes.

Aim The aim of our study was to evaluate the efficacy and the safety of high-dose SLIT given pre-seasonally and co-seasonally in an ultra-rush scheme in children with bronchial asthma allergic to grass pollen.
